questions.q: Scenario: User A is in Group X (Reader on subscription) and Group Y (Contributor on rg-data). Can A delete a VM in rg-data?
questions.why: Effective permissions are the union; Contributor on rg-data allows it (unless a lock or deny assignment blocks it).

questions.q: Scenario: blobs must be cheap to store, read about once a year, and retrieval within a few hours is fine. Tier?
questions.why: For data read about once a year, where retrieval in hours is fine, the Archive tier is the cheapest. Its data must be rehydrated before reading.

questions.q: Scenario: dynamic membership rules cannot be created. What should you check first?
options: Whether the tenant has Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher
questions.why: Dynamic group membership requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or higher. If you cannot create dynamic rules, check the tenant's licence first.

questions.q: Scenario: a script must list storage account keys, but fails with an authorisation error even though you are Owner. A lock is on the account. Which lock?
questions.why: A ReadOnly lock blocks the POST operation that lists storage account keys, even for an Owner. A CanNotDelete lock does not.

questions.q: Scenario: you need read access to the secondary region at all times, plus protection from a zone failure in the primary. Choose…
questions.why: RA-GZRS has zone-redundant storage in the primary region, a geo copy in the secondary and read access to the secondary. RA-GRS lacks the zone protection in the primary.

questions.q: Scenario: existing resources lack a required tag. You assign a Modify policy. What else is needed to fix existing resources?
questions.why: A Modify policy only acts on resources that are created or updated after assignment. To fix existing non-compliant resources, you must also run a remediation task.

questions.q: Scenario: operators must start and stop VMs in one resource group only, nothing else. Best solution?
options: Custom role with start/restart/deallocate actions, assigned at that resource group to a group
questions.why: Least privilege means giving only the needed actions at the smallest scope. A custom role with start, restart and deallocate, assigned to a group at that one resource group, does exactly that. Owner or subscription Contributor is far too broad.

questions.q: Scenario: a contractor received an account-key SAS with no expiry; you must cut access immediately, and other apps use key 2. Best action?
options: Regenerate key 1 (the key used to sign the SAS)
questions.why: A SAS from an account key is signed with that key. Regenerating key 1 invalidates the SAS tokens signed with it, while apps using key 2 keep working.

questions.q: Scenario: Azure File Sync — you add a second Windows Server in another branch to the same sync group. What do you create?
options: A new server endpoint on the registered server
A new Storage Sync Service per server
questions.why: A sync group has one cloud endpoint (the Azure file share) and can have many server endpoints. For the new server, register it and create a new server endpoint on it.

courses.title: Azure administrator II: compute, networking, monitoring and backup (AZ-104 style)
courses.summary: For mid-senior engineers preparing for the administrator exam: virtual machines and availability, templates, App Service and containers, virtual networks, NSGs, peering, load balancing, DNS and hybrid connectivity, Azure Monitor and backup/recovery — with scenario questions. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can deploy and manage VMs, disks, availability sets/zones and scale sets, including with ARM/Bicep templates
Learners can configure App Service plans, deployment slots and container services
Learners can design VNets and subnets, NSGs/ASGs, peering, routes and private access
Learners can choose between Load Balancer, Application Gateway and other traffic services and configure DNS and hybrid links
Learners can monitor with metrics, logs, KQL and alerts, and protect workloads with Azure Backup and Site Recovery

lessons.title: Virtual machines, availability and templates

story.title: The patch night that took the site down

scenes.text: A travel booking company in Jaipur ran its web tier on two VMs. During a platform maintenance event both VMs rebooted together — the site was down for 20 minutes during peak booking.
Cloud engineer Vikram found the VMs were not in an availability set or across zones, so nothing stopped them sharing the same hardware and update schedule.
He redeployed with a Bicep template: VMs across availability zones behind a load balancer, managed disks, and a scale set for peak season.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. SLA numbers and feature details change — always verify in current documentation.

steps.title: VM essentials
steps.body:
- **Size families** (general purpose, compute, memory, storage, GPU). Resizing restarts the VM; if the new size isn't available on the current hardware cluster you must **deallocate** first.
- **Stopped vs deallocated:** shutting down inside the OS leaves the VM allocated (compute still billed). **Stop (deallocate)** from Azure releases compute (disks still billed).
- **Managed disks:** Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2, Ultra Disk. Data is encrypted at rest by default (server-side encryption with platform-managed keys); options include customer-managed keys, **encryption at host**, and **Azure Disk Encryption** (BitLocker/DM-Crypt inside the guest).
- Connect securely with **Azure Bastion** (RDP/SSH through the browser, no public IP on the VM) or just-in-time VM access.

steps.title: Availability options
steps.body:
- **Availability set:** spreads VMs across **fault domains** (separate racks/power — up to 3) and **update domains** (rebooted at different times during planned maintenance — up to 20, default 5). Protects against hardware failure and maintenance within a data centre.
- **Availability zones:** VMs in separate data centres within a region — protects against a data-centre failure.
- **Virtual Machine Scale Sets:** identical (or flexible) VMs with **autoscale** rules (e.g. add 2 instances when average CPU > 70% for 10 minutes).
Indicative VM SLAs (check current terms): two or more VMs across zones 99.99%; in an availability set 99.95%; a single VM with Premium SSD/Ultra disks 99.9%.

steps.title: ARM templates and Bicep
steps.body:
Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable.
- **ARM template (JSON):** sections $schema, contentVersion, parameters, variables, resources, outputs (functions and user-defined functions optional).
- **Bicep:** a simpler language that compiles to ARM JSON.
- Deployment scopes: resource group, subscription, management group, tenant.
- **Deployment modes:** **Incremental** (default — adds/updates, leaves other resources) vs **Complete** (deletes resources in the resource group not in the template).
- Export a template from an existing resource group or a past deployment; deploy with portal, CLI (az deployment group create), or PowerShell.

steps.title: Worked example: a minimal Bicep storage account
Try this
steps.body: Deploy a small Linux VM with no public IP, connect through Bastion, resize it, then stop (deallocate) it and check billing behaviour in Cost Management the next day.

a.text: You are Vikram. The web tier must survive the failure of an entire data centre in Central India. Which design?

choices.label: VMs across availability zones behind a Standard Load Balancer
choices.feedback: Correct — zones isolate data-centre failures.

choices.label: Two VMs in an availability set
choices.feedback: An availability set protects within a data centre, not against losing it.

b.text: Traffic triples in December. You want instances added automatically based on CPU. Use…

choices.label: A Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules
choices.feedback: Yes — scale out and in automatically.

choices.label: Resize each VM to a bigger size manually
choices.feedback: Vertical scaling needs restarts and doesn't react automatically.

c.text: A cooling failure takes one data centre offline; both VMs are in it. The site goes down.

choices.label: Redesign across availability zones
choices.feedback: Right lesson.

c2.text: Each resize restarts a VM during peak hours.

choices.label: Move to a scale set with autoscale
choices.feedback: Horizontal, automatic scaling.

d.text: Zone-redundant scale set behind a Standard Load Balancer, defined in Bicep, deployed in Incremental mode through a pipeline. Resilient and repeatable.

quiz.q: Maximum number of fault domains in an availability set (typical)?
quiz.why: An availability set spreads VMs across up to 3 fault domains (typical), which are like separate racks with their own power and network.

quiz.q: You shut down a VM from inside Windows. Is compute still billed?
quiz.why: Shutting down from inside Windows leaves the VM allocated, so compute is still billed. You must stop (deallocate) it from Azure to stop compute charges.

quiz.q: A template deployment in Complete mode will…
options: Delete resources in the resource group not defined in the template
quiz.why: In Complete mode, Azure Resource Manager deletes resources in the resource group that are not defined in the template. Incremental mode only adds or updates, so be careful with Complete.

quiz.q: Resizing fails because the size isn't available on the current cluster. Next step?
quiz.why: If a size isn't available on the current hardware cluster, deallocate the VM first and then resize. This lets Azure place it on a cluster that supports the new size.

quiz.q: RDP to VMs without public IPs, through the browser. Use…
quiz.why: Azure Bastion gives secure RDP or SSH to VMs through the browser, over TLS, without public IPs on the VMs.

lessons.title: App Service and containers

story.title: Zero-downtime releases for an exam-results site

scenes.text: A state education board's results website crashed every year on results day, and each release needed a late-night outage.
Engineer Lakshmi moved it to App Service on a Premium plan with autoscale, and used a staging slot: deploy, warm up, test, then swap into production in seconds.
A background PDF-generation service went into Azure Container Apps, scaling with the queue length.

steps.title: App Service plans
steps.body:
An **App Service plan** defines the region, the OS, and the compute (tier and instance size) that apps in it share. Tiers: Free, Shared, Basic, Standard, Premium, Isolated.
- **Scale up:** move to a bigger tier/size (more CPU, memory, features).
- **Scale out:** more instances — manual or **autoscale** (Standard tier and above).
- **Deployment slots** (Standard and above): staging, testing etc. **Swap** a warmed-up slot into production; swap back to roll back. Some settings can be marked **slot-specific** (sticky) so they don't move during swaps (e.g. a staging database connection string).
- Other features: custom domains and TLS certificates, backups, VNet integration for outbound access to private resources, private endpoints for inbound private access, authentication (Easy Auth).

steps.title: Container services
steps.body:
- **Azure Container Registry (ACR):** private registry for images (Basic, Standard, Premium; Premium adds geo-replication and private link). Build images in the cloud with ACR Tasks.
- **Azure Container Instances (ACI):** run a single container or container group quickly, billed per second; no orchestration.
- **Azure Container Apps:** serverless containers with autoscaling (including to zero) based on HTTP traffic, events or queues; revisions and traffic splitting.
- **AKS:** managed Kubernetes for full control over complex microservice platforms (see the DevOps course).

steps.title: Worked example: a slot swap with sticky settings
steps.body:
- Production slot: setting DB_CONN = prod-db (marked as deployment-slot setting).
- Staging slot: DB_CONN = staging-db (also slot setting).
- Deploy v2 to staging; test against staging-db.
- Swap: the v2 code moves to production; DB_CONN stays with each slot, so production v2 uses prod-db. If v2 misbehaves, swap again to roll back to v1.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Trying to add slots or autoscale on Basic — not available.
- Forgetting that all apps in a plan share its instances — a noisy app slows the others.
- Pulling from ACR without permission: grant the AcrPull role to the managed identity of the app/cluster.
- Assuming ACI is for long-running, auto-scaled production microservices — consider Container Apps or AKS.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a Standard App Service plan, deploy a sample app, add a staging slot, change a page, swap, and then swap back. Mark one setting as a slot setting and observe it stay put.

activity.prompt: Match the need to the service or feature.
pairs: Test a release, then switch it into production in seconds
Run one container for a short batch job, billed per second
Serverless containers that scale with queue length, even to zero
Full Kubernetes control for many microservices

quiz.q: Minimum App Service tier for deployment slots?
quiz.why: Deployment slots need the Standard App Service tier or higher. Free, Shared and Basic do not support them.

quiz.q: Scaling out an App Service plan means…
quiz.why: Scaling out means adding more instances of the plan. Scaling up means a bigger instance size.

quiz.q: A connection string must stay with the staging slot during swaps. Mark it as…
quiz.why: Mark a setting as a deployment slot setting (sticky) so it stays with the slot and is not swapped with the app.

quiz.q: An App Service app must pull images from ACR without passwords. Grant its managed identity…
quiz.why: AcrPull is the Azure Container Registry role that allows pulling images. Give it to the app's managed identity, so no password is needed.

quiz.q: Apps in the same plan…
quiz.why: All apps in an App Service plan share the plan's compute instances. The plan defines the VMs, region and size.

lessons.title: Virtual networks, NSGs, peering and routing

story.title: The database that could be reached from the internet

scenes.text: A security scan flagged that a health-tech company's database VM in Bengaluru accepted connections from any internet address on port 1433.
Network admin Ayesha redesigned the VNet: web, app and data subnets; NSGs allowing only web → app → data; no public IPs on app or data VMs.
A shared-services VNet (DNS, firewall) was peered with the app VNet. When a third VNet couldn't reach the second, she remembered: peering is not transitive.

steps.title: VNets and subnets
steps.body:
- A **VNet** has one or more address spaces (private ranges such as 10.0.0.0/16). Subnets divide it (10.0.1.0/24).
- Azure **reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet**: the network address, the default gateway (.1), two for Azure DNS mapping (.2, .3), and the broadcast address (last). A /24 therefore has 256 − 5 = **251** usable addresses; /29 is the smallest supported IPv4 subnet (3 usable).
- Special subnets: **GatewaySubnet** (VPN/ExpressRoute gateways), **AzureBastionSubnet** (/26 or larger), **AzureFirewallSubnet**.
- Address spaces of VNets you plan to connect (peering, VPN) must **not overlap**.
- Public IP SKUs: use **Standard** (secure by default, zone-capable).

steps.title: Network security groups (NSGs) and ASGs
steps.body:
- An **NSG** contains rules: priority (100–4096; **lower number = evaluated first**), source, destination, port, protocol, Allow/Deny. The first matching rule wins.
- Default rules (priority 65000+) allow traffic within the VNet and from the Azure load balancer, and deny all other inbound; outbound to the internet is allowed by default.
- Associate NSGs with **subnets** and/or **NICs**. For inbound traffic the subnet NSG is evaluated first, then the NIC NSG; for outbound, NIC then subnet. Traffic must be allowed by both.
- **Application security groups (ASGs)** let you write rules using names such as 'asg-web' instead of IP addresses.
- Use **Effective security rules** and Network Watcher **IP flow verify** to troubleshoot.

steps.title: Peering and routing
steps.body:
- **VNet peering** (regional or global) connects VNets over Microsoft's backbone with low latency. **Not transitive:** if A↔B and B↔C, A cannot reach C unless A↔C are peered or traffic is routed through a network virtual appliance/firewall in B.
- **Gateway transit:** a peered VNet can use the hub's VPN gateway ('Allow gateway transit' on the hub, 'Use remote gateways' on the spoke).
- **User-defined routes (UDRs):** route tables override system routes — e.g. send 0.0.0.0/0 to a firewall (next hop type **Virtual appliance**). Other next hop types: Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, Internet, None.
- **Hub-and-spoke** topology: shared services in the hub; spokes peered to it.

steps.title: Worked example: rule evaluation
steps.body:
Inbound NSG on the data subnet:
- 100: Allow TCP 1433 from asg-app
- 200: Deny TCP 1433 from Any
- 65000+: defaults
A packet from an app VM (member of asg-app) on 1433 → matches rule 100 → **allowed** (rule 200 never checked).
A packet from the web subnet on 1433 → not in asg-app → rule 200 → **denied**.
If someone adds '150: Allow Any 1433 from Internet', traffic from the internet is allowed — because 150 is evaluated before 200. Order matters.

steps.title: Private access to PaaS
steps.body:
- **Service endpoints:** extend the subnet identity to a PaaS service over the backbone; the service keeps its public endpoint but can restrict access to that subnet.
- **Private endpoints (Private Link):** a NIC with a private IP in your subnet for a specific resource; combine with **private DNS zones** (e.g. privatelink.blob.core.windows.net) linked to the VNet; public access can be disabled.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Calculate usable addresses for /26, /27 and /28 subnets in Azure. (Answers: 64−5 = 59, 32−5 = 27, 16−5 = 11.)

activity.prompt: How many usable IP addresses does Azure give you in a /25 subnet?

quiz.q: NSG rules with priorities 300 (Deny) and 200 (Allow) both match. Result?
quiz.why: NSG rules are evaluated in order of priority number, with the lowest number first. The Allow at 200 is processed before the Deny at 300, so traffic is allowed.

quiz.q: VNet A is peered with B, and B with C. Can A reach C by default?
quiz.why: VNet peering is not transitive. A can't reach C through B by default; you'd need a direct A–C peering or a routing appliance in B.

quiz.q: Name of the subnet required for a VPN gateway?
quiz.why: A VPN gateway needs a dedicated subnet that is named exactly GatewaySubnet.

quiz.q: Send all internet-bound traffic through a firewall. Use…
options: User-defined route with next hop Virtual appliance
quiz.why: A user-defined route (UDR) with 0.0.0.0/0 and next hop type 'Virtual appliance', pointing to the firewall's IP, forces internet-bound traffic through the firewall.

quiz.q: Peering fails to create. Most common cause?
quiz.why: VNet peering requires non-overlapping address spaces. Overlapping ranges are the most common cause of peering failures.

lessons.title: Load balancing, DNS and hybrid connectivity

story.title: One URL, many servers, two offices

scenes.text: An e-commerce firm in Mumbai needed /images traffic to go to one pool of servers and /checkout to another, with protection from web attacks.
Network architect Rohit chose Application Gateway with WAF for path-based routing, and a Standard Load Balancer for the internal app tier.
The Delhi warehouse connected via site-to-site VPN; head office, with heavy, steady traffic, used ExpressRoute. Private DNS zones let VMs find each other by name.

steps.title: Choosing a traffic service
steps.body:
- **Azure Load Balancer (layer 4, TCP/UDP):** public or internal; distributes by a hash of source/destination IP and ports; **health probes**; load-balancing rules and inbound NAT rules. Use the **Standard** SKU (zone-redundant, secure by default, SLA).
- **Application Gateway (layer 7, HTTP/HTTPS) — regional:** URL path-based and multi-site routing, TLS termination, cookie-based session affinity, autoscaling, optional **Web Application Firewall (WAF)**.
- **Azure Front Door (layer 7) — global:** edge entry point, global HTTP load balancing, caching, WAF.
- **Traffic Manager — DNS-based global routing:** priority, weighted, performance, geographic routing methods; it does not proxy traffic.
Rule of thumb: regional + non-HTTP → Load Balancer; regional + HTTP features → Application Gateway; global HTTP → Front Door; global DNS steering of any protocol → Traffic Manager.

steps.title: Azure DNS
steps.body:
- **Public DNS zones:** host your domain's records (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, etc.) on Azure name servers; delegate the domain at your registrar by updating NS records.
- **Private DNS zones:** name resolution inside VNets; link the zone to VNets, optionally with **auto-registration** so VM records are created automatically.
- VNets can use Azure-provided DNS or custom DNS servers.

steps.title: Hybrid connectivity
steps.body:
- **Site-to-site VPN:** IPsec/IKE tunnel from an on-premises VPN device to an Azure VPN gateway, over the internet. Needs the GatewaySubnet, a local network gateway (on-premises public IP and address ranges) and a connection.
- **Point-to-site VPN:** individual devices connect (e.g. a remote admin's laptop).
- **VNet-to-VNet:** VPN between VNets (peering is usually simpler).
- **ExpressRoute:** private connection through a connectivity provider; predictable performance; does not traverse the public internet (encryption is still your choice, e.g. MACsec or IPsec over it). A VPN can serve as a backup path.
- **Azure Virtual WAN:** a managed hub for large branch networks.

steps.title: Worked example: health probes
steps.body:
An internal Standard Load Balancer has a backend pool of 3 app VMs, a health probe on HTTP /health port 8080 every 5 seconds, and a rule TCP 443 → 8443.
If VM2's app crashes, /health fails, the probe marks VM2 unhealthy and new flows go only to VM1 and VM3. When VM2 recovers, it rejoins automatically. Common outage cause: the NSG blocks the probe source — allow the AzureLoadBalancer service tag.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Using Load Balancer when you need URL path routing or WAF (needs Application Gateway / Front Door).
- Forgetting to update the registrar's NS records after creating a public zone.
- Overlapping on-premises and VNet address ranges, which breaks VPN routing.
- Assuming Traffic Manager sees HTTP paths — it only answers DNS queries.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For each, pick the service: (1) global website with caching and WAF; (2) internal SQL Always On listener; (3) /api and /images to different pools in one region; (4) failover between two regions for a non-HTTP game server. (Answers: Front Door, internal Load Balancer, Application Gateway, Traffic Manager.)

activity.prompt: Which traffic service fits?

items.text: Regional TCP load balancing for a game server
Route /checkout and /images to different backends in one region with WAF
Global HTTP entry point with edge caching
Internal load balancing for an app tier
TLS termination and cookie-based affinity for a regional web app

quiz.q: Which service supports URL path-based routing within a region?
quiz.why: Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer that supports URL path-based routing. Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4.

quiz.q: Traffic Manager routes users by…
quiz.why: Traffic Manager is DNS-based: it answers DNS queries with the endpoint chosen by the routing method. It does not proxy traffic.

quiz.q: VMs in a VNet should get DNS records automatically in a private zone. Enable…
options: Auto-registration on the virtual network link
quiz.why: Auto-registration on the virtual network link in a private DNS zone creates and removes DNS records for the VMs in that VNet automatically.

quiz.q: Which hybrid option avoids the public internet?
quiz.why: ExpressRoute is a private connection through a provider and avoids the public internet. Site-to-site and point-to-site VPNs use the internet.

quiz.q: All backend VMs show unhealthy, but apps run fine. Likely cause?
quiz.why: If every backend VM shows unhealthy while the apps run fine, an NSG may be blocking the health probe. Allow the AzureLoadBalancer service tag on the probe port.

lessons.title: Monitoring, alerts, backup and recovery

scenes.text: A clinic chain in Kerala found its file server encrypted by ransomware on a Sunday morning.

Thankfully, administrator Thomas had Azure Backup for the VMs with daily backups, soft delete and multi-user authorisation for critical operations. The attackers' attempt to delete backups was blocked.
He restored the VM from Friday night's recovery point within hours. Afterwards he added alerts for unusual sign-ins, CPU spikes and backup failures, all sent to an on-call action group.

steps.title: Azure Monitor building blocks
steps.body:
- **Metrics:** numeric time series (CPU %, disk IOPS), near real time, retained for a limited period by default.
- **Logs:** records stored in a **Log Analytics workspace**, queried with **KQL** (Kusto Query Language).
- **Activity log:** subscription-level 'who did what and when' for control-plane operations.
- **Diagnostic settings:** send resource logs and metrics to Log Analytics, a storage account or Event Hubs.
- **Azure Monitor Agent** with **data collection rules** collects guest OS logs and performance data from VMs.
- **Insights:** VM insights, Container insights, Network insights; **Application Insights** for app telemetry.

steps.title: Worked example: KQL queries
steps.body:
Which VMs stopped sending heartbeats in the last 15 minutes?
Heartbeat
| summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where LastSeen < ago(15m)

Top 5 VMs by average CPU in the last hour:
Perf
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) and ObjectName == 'Processor' and CounterName == '% Processor Time'
| summarize AvgCPU = avg(CounterValue) by Computer
| top 5 by AvgCPU desc

(Table names depend on what you collect; newer agents may send performance data to InsightsMetrics or other tables.)

steps.title: Alerts and action groups
steps.body:
- **Alert rule** = scope (resource) + condition (metric, log search, or activity log signal) + **action group**.
- **Action groups:** who/what to notify — email, SMS, push, voice — and automation: webhook, Logic App, Azure Function, Automation runbook, ITSM.
- **Alert processing rules:** suppress notifications during planned maintenance or add action groups at scale.
- Severity levels 0 (critical) to 4 (verbose). Design alerts that are actionable — too many alerts train people to ignore them.

steps.title: Azure Backup and Site Recovery
steps.body:
- **Recovery Services vault:** backup of Azure VMs, SQL Server/SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, and on-premises files via the MARS agent; also hosts **Azure Site Recovery**.
- **Backup vault:** newer workloads such as Azure Blobs, Azure Disks and Azure Database for PostgreSQL.
- For Azure VM backup, the vault must be in the **same region** as the VM.
- **Backup policy:** schedule (daily/weekly or more frequent options for some workloads) and retention (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly).
- **Soft delete** keeps deleted backup data for a retention period (14 days by default) — vital against ransomware; plus **immutable vaults** and **multi-user authorisation**.
- Restore options for VMs: create a new VM, restore disks, replace existing disks, or file-level recovery.
- **Cross Region Restore** is available when the vault uses geo-redundant storage.
- **Azure Site Recovery (ASR):** continuous replication of VMs to another region for **disaster recovery**; run test failovers without affecting production. Backup = recover data to a point in time; Site Recovery = keep the business running elsewhere (low RPO/RTO).

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body:
- Creating the vault in a different region from the VMs.
- Never testing restores — a backup you haven't restored is a hope, not a plan.
- A vault can't be deleted while it still contains protected items or soft-deleted backup data.
- Confusing the activity log (control-plane operations) with guest OS logs.
- Alerting only by email to one person who is on leave — use action groups with on-call rotations.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Back up a test VM, delete a file inside it, then use file-level recovery to get it back. Create a metric alert for CPU > 80% for 5 minutes with an action group that emails you, and trigger it with a stress tool.

a.text: You are Thomas. You must back up VMs in South India. Where do you create the Recovery Services vault?

choices.label: In South India, the same region as the VMs
choices.feedback: Correct — Azure VM backup needs the vault in the same region.

choices.label: In Central India for safety
choices.feedback: For VM backup, the vault must be in the VM's region. Use GRS/Cross Region Restore for geo-protection.

b.text: An attacker with stolen admin credentials tries to delete backups. Which features help most?

choices.label: Soft delete, immutable vault and multi-user authorisation
choices.feedback: Layered protection for backups.

choices.label: Tags on the vault
choices.feedback: Tags organise; they don't protect.

c.text: The VMs don't appear as backup items in the other region's vault.

choices.label: Create the vault in South India
choices.feedback: Fixed.

c2.text: Without protection, the attacker could have removed recovery points.

choices.label: Enable soft delete, immutability and MUA
choices.feedback: Now deletion needs extra approval and is recoverable.

d.text: Backups protected, restores tested monthly, alerts routed to an on-call action group, and Site Recovery replicating critical VMs to another region. Ready for a bad Sunday.

quiz.q: Which language queries Log Analytics?
quiz.why: Log Analytics is queried with KQL (Kusto Query Language).

quiz.q: Who deleted a VM yesterday? Check the…
quiz.why: Control-plane operations such as deleting a VM are recorded in the Activity log. It shows who did it and when.

quiz.q: An alert must send an SMS and run a runbook. Configure…
quiz.why: An action group defines the notifications (such as SMS) and actions (such as running a runbook) that an alert triggers.

quiz.q: Default soft-delete retention for Azure Backup data (typical)?
quiz.why: Azure Backup soft delete keeps deleted backup data for 14 days by default, so it can be recovered.

quiz.q: Keep a business app running in another region if the primary region fails, with minimal data loss. Use…
quiz.why: Azure Site Recovery replicates workloads to another region for disaster recovery, so the app can fail over with minimal data loss. Backup alone restores data but does not give quick failover.

questions.q: Which load balancer works at layer 4?
questions.why: Azure Load Balancer works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP). Application Gateway and Front Door work at layer 7.

questions.q: Which vault type backs up Azure VMs?
questions.why: A Recovery Services vault stores Azure VM backups and recovery points. A Key Vault is for secrets.

questions.q: How many IPs does Azure reserve in each subnet?
questions.why: Azure reserves 5 IP addresses in each subnet: the network address, broadcast address, and three for Azure services (gateway and DNS).

questions.q: Lower NSG priority numbers are evaluated…
questions.why: Lower NSG priority numbers are evaluated first, so priority 100 is checked before 4096.

questions.q: Which feature lets you test a new web app version and swap it into production?
questions.why: Deployment slots let you deploy and test a new version in a staging slot, then swap it into production.

questions.q: Scenario: two VMs must be protected against rack-level hardware failure and planned maintenance in one data centre at low cost. Use…
questions.why: An availability set spreads VMs over fault domains and update domains inside one data centre. It protects against rack failure and planned maintenance at low cost. Availability zones protect against whole data-centre failure.

questions.q: Scenario: a /27 subnet — how many VMs can get private IPs?
questions.why: A /27 has 32 addresses. Azure reserves 5, so 32 − 5 = 27 are usable for VMs.

questions.q: Scenario: spoke VNets must use the hub's VPN gateway to reach on-premises. Configure…
options: Gateway transit on the hub peering and 'use remote gateways' on spokes
A public IP on each VM
questions.why: For spokes to use the hub's VPN gateway, allow gateway transit on the hub side of the peering and enable 'use remote gateways' on the spokes' peerings.

questions.q: Scenario: an App Service on the Basic tier needs autoscale. What must you do?
options: Scale up the plan to Standard or higher
questions.why: Autoscale needs the Standard tier or higher. Basic only supports manual scaling, so scale up the plan first.

questions.q: Scenario: inbound NSG on subnet allows TCP 443; NIC NSG has no rule for 443 (only defaults). Is internet traffic on 443 allowed to the VM?
options: No — the NIC NSG's default DenyAllInBound blocks it
questions.why: Traffic must be allowed by both NSGs (the subnet and the NIC). The NIC NSG has no allow for 443, so its default DenyAllInBound blocks it.

questions.q: Scenario: a deployment in Complete mode removed a storage account. Why?
options: It was in the resource group but not in the template
questions.why: In Complete mode, resources in the resource group that are not in the template are deleted. The storage account was in the group but missing from the template.

questions.q: Scenario: VNets A (10.1.0.0/16) and B (10.1.0.0/24) cannot be peered. Fix?
options: Re-address one VNet so ranges do not overlap
questions.why: 10.1.0.0/24 lies inside 10.1.0.0/16, so the address spaces overlap and peering is blocked. Re-address one VNet so the ranges don't overlap.

questions.q: Scenario: you need a query of VMs that have not sent a heartbeat for 15 minutes, with an alert. Use…
options: Log search alert using a KQL query on the Heartbeat table
questions.why: A log search alert uses a KQL query on the Heartbeat table to find VMs with no heartbeat in 15 minutes. A CPU metric alert or an activity log alert doesn't check this.

questions.q: Scenario: a storage account must be reachable only privately from a VNet with no public access, and names must resolve correctly. Configure…
options: Private endpoint + private DNS zone linked to the VNet + disable public network access
questions.why: For private-only access, use a private endpoint, a private DNS zone linked to the VNet so the name resolves to the private IP, and disable public network access. A service endpoint alone does not give a private IP.

questions.q: Scenario: VM backups must be restorable in the paired region if the primary region is unavailable. Configure…
options: GRS vault with Cross Region Restore enabled
A second vault in the same region
questions.why: Cross Region Restore lets you restore backups in the paired region. It needs a geo-redundant (GRS) vault with the feature enabled.

courses.title: Beyond admin: Azure developer (AZ-204) and Azure AI engineer (AI-102) overview
courses.summary: A map of what developers and AI engineers build on Azure: compute and storage for apps, security with managed identities and Key Vault, messaging and APIs, monitoring — and Azure AI services, Azure OpenAI, AI Search and responsible AI. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can describe the main service areas a developer exam typically covers and pick services for a scenario
Learners can choose between Event Grid, Event Hubs, Service Bus and Queue Storage
Learners can secure apps with managed identities and Key Vault
Learners can map AI scenarios to Azure AI services, Azure OpenAI and AI Search and plan hands-on study

lessons.title: Developer path: building apps on Azure

story.title: An order pipeline for a D2C brand

scenes.text: A skincare brand in Bengaluru was growing fast. Every order needed payment confirmation, an invoice PDF, warehouse notification and an SMS.
Developer Arnav built it on Azure: an App Service API, an Azure Function triggered by new orders, Service Bus queues between steps, Cosmos DB for orders, Blob Storage for invoices.
No passwords lived in code: each component used a managed identity, and secrets that had to exist lived in Key Vault.

steps.title: About this course
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline. Exam codes, outlines and even whole exams change or are retired over time — check the official exam page before you plan your study.

steps.title: Compute for developers
steps.body:
- **App Service:** web apps and APIs; deployment slots, autoscale, settings, logging.
- **Azure Functions:** event-driven code. A function has exactly one **trigger** (HTTP, timer, queue, blob, Event Grid, Service Bus, Cosmos DB…) and optional input/output **bindings** that connect to data without boilerplate. Hosting options include consumption-style serverless plans and dedicated/premium plans; durable functions orchestrate long workflows.
- **Containers:** build and push images to Azure Container Registry; run on Container Apps or Container Instances.

steps.title: Storage and data for apps
steps.body:
- **Blob Storage** via SDKs: containers, blobs, metadata, access tiers, lifecycle.
- **Azure Cosmos DB:** globally distributed NoSQL database; choose a **partition key** with high cardinality and even access; five consistency levels from strong to eventual (strong, bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix, eventual); throughput measured in request units (RUs); change feed for event-driven processing.

steps.title: Security for developers
steps.body:
- **Microsoft identity platform / MSAL:** sign users in and get tokens (OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect).
- **Managed identities:** system-assigned (tied to one resource's lifecycle) or user-assigned (standalone, shareable) identities that let code get tokens for Azure services without secrets.
- **Azure Key Vault:** store secrets, keys and certificates; access via RBAC; soft delete and purge protection.
- **App Configuration:** central feature flags and settings.
- **Shared access signatures** for delegated storage access.

steps.title: Messaging, APIs and monitoring
steps.body:
- **Queue Storage:** simple, very large queues of messages.
- **Service Bus:** enterprise messaging — queues and topics/subscriptions, sessions (ordering), dead-letter queues, duplicate detection, transactions.
- **Event Grid:** reactive event routing (a blob was created, a resource changed) with publish–subscribe and filtering.
- **Event Hubs:** high-throughput event streaming/telemetry ingestion (millions of events), partitions and consumer groups.
- **API Management:** a gateway in front of APIs — policies for rate limiting, authentication, transformation, caching, and a developer portal.
- **Application Insights:** requests, dependencies, exceptions, traces, availability tests, distributed tracing.

steps.title: Worked example: picking the messaging service
steps.body:
- 'Order placed' must be processed exactly in order per customer, with retries and dead-lettering → **Service Bus** queue with sessions.
- React when an invoice PDF lands in Blob Storage → **Event Grid** (blob created event) → Function.
- 50,000 IoT temperature readings per second from cold-storage trucks → **Event Hubs**.
- A simple background-work queue with millions of small jobs, minimal features → **Queue Storage**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Build a Function with an HTTP trigger that writes a message to a queue (output binding), and a second Function with a queue trigger that writes a blob. Give the Function App a managed identity and remove any connection-string secrets you can.

activity.prompt: Match the scenario to the Azure service.
pairs: Millions of telemetry events per second
Store API keys and certificates securely
Globally distributed NoSQL with tunable consistency

quiz.q: How many triggers can one Azure Function have?
quiz.why: An Azure Function has exactly one trigger, which starts it. It can have many input and output bindings.

quiz.q: Code needs a token for Storage without any stored secret. Use…
quiz.why: A managed identity lets code get a token for Storage without any stored secret. Account keys and SAS tokens must be stored and can leak.

quiz.q: Which Cosmos DB consistency level is the strongest?
quiz.why: Strong is the strictest Cosmos DB consistency level: reads always see the latest committed write. Eventual is the weakest.

quiz.q: High-volume telemetry ingestion from IoT devices — choose…
quiz.why: Event Hubs is built for high-volume streaming ingestion, like IoT telemetry. Queue Storage is simpler and not meant for this scale.

quiz.q: A user-assigned managed identity is…
options: A standalone identity that can be shared by several resources
quiz.why: A user-assigned managed identity is created separately, has its own lifecycle and can be shared by several resources. A system-assigned one is tied to a single resource and deleted with it.

lessons.title: AI engineer path: Azure AI services, Azure OpenAI and AI Search

scenes.text: A state welfare department receives lakhs of paper application forms, partly handwritten, in English and Hindi.

AI engineer Zainab designed a pipeline: Document Intelligence extracts fields, the Language service detects personal data, AI Search indexes the documents, and an Azure OpenAI model answers officers' questions with citations.
She added content safety filters, kept humans approving every benefit decision, and documented the system's limits.

steps.title: The AI service families
steps.body:
Azure offers prebuilt AI capabilities through APIs and SDKs (product names change often — for example, Cognitive Services became Azure AI services, Cognitive Search became Azure AI Search, and Form Recognizer became Document Intelligence):
- **Vision:** image analysis, OCR (read text), face-related features (restricted access), custom image models.
- **Language:** sentiment, key phrases, named entities, PII detection, summarisation, custom text classification, conversational language understanding, question answering.
- **Speech:** speech-to-text, text-to-speech, speech translation.
- **Translator:** text and document translation.
- **Document Intelligence:** extract text, key-value pairs, tables and fields from forms, invoices, receipts, IDs; custom models.
- **Content Safety:** detect harmful text and images.
- **Azure OpenAI / foundation models:** chat and completion models, embeddings, image generation, used through a studio/portal and APIs.

steps.title: Azure AI Search
steps.body:
- An **index** holds searchable documents with fields (searchable, filterable, facetable, sortable, retrievable).
- **Indexers** pull data from sources such as Blob Storage, SQL and Cosmos DB on a schedule.
- **Skillsets** enrich content during indexing (OCR, language detection, entity extraction, chunking and embedding).
- Query types: keyword (full text), **vector**, **hybrid**, and **semantic ranking**.
- It is a common retrieval layer for RAG solutions with Azure OpenAI (see the AI engineer pack's RAG lesson).

steps.title: Securing and operating AI resources
steps.body:
- Prefer Microsoft Entra authentication and managed identities over API keys; if keys are used, store them in Key Vault and rotate.
- Network isolation with private endpoints; disable public access where possible.
- Monitor usage, latency and errors; manage quotas and cost (tokens, transactions).
- Choose regions that offer the models and data-residency you need.
- Single-service vs multi-service resources: one key/endpoint for many services is convenient; separate resources give finer control and billing.

steps.title: Responsible AI on the platform
steps.body:
- Content filters for prompts and completions, with configurable severity thresholds.
- Some capabilities (for example certain face features) require approved access and have usage restrictions.
- Transparency notes describe intended uses and limitations of services.
- Human oversight for consequential decisions; evaluate for fairness and groundedness; red-team generative apps; document your system.

steps.title: Worked example: mapping Zainab's needs
steps.body:
- Extract applicant name, Aadhaar-masked ID field, income and address from scanned forms → **Document Intelligence** (prebuilt or custom model).
- Detect and redact personal data before analytics → **Language: PII detection**.
- Let officers search 'widow pension applications from Barmer in March' → **AI Search** with filters and hybrid search.
- Answer 'What documents are missing for application 4821?' with citations → **Azure OpenAI** model + AI Search retrieval (RAG).
- Block abusive inputs and outputs → **Content Safety** / content filters.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a one-page design for an AI assistant at your college or office: which Azure AI services you'd use, how data flows, where humans approve, and which risks you'd test before launch.

activity.prompt: Which Azure AI capability fits each task?

items.text: Pull totals and GST numbers from scanned invoices
Detect personal data in customer emails
Hybrid keyword + vector search over 1 million PDFs
Draft answers to policy questions grounded in retrieved passages

quiz.q: Extracting key-value pairs and tables from forms is the job of…
quiz.why: Document Intelligence (formerly Form Recognizer) extracts key-value pairs, tables and text from forms and documents.

quiz.q: In AI Search, what pulls data from Blob Storage on a schedule?
quiz.why: An indexer in Azure AI Search pulls data from a source such as Blob Storage on a schedule and fills the index.

quiz.q: Skillsets in AI Search are used to…
options: Enrich content during indexing (OCR, entities, embeddings)
quiz.why: A skillset enriches content during indexing, for example with OCR, entity extraction or embeddings.

quiz.q: Most secure way for an app to call an Azure AI resource?
options: Shared key on a sticky note
Microsoft Entra authentication with a managed identity
quiz.why: Microsoft Entra authentication with a managed identity leaves no secrets to leak. Keys in code or on notes can be stolen.

quiz.q: Detecting harmful text or images in a generative app uses…
quiz.why: Azure AI Content Safety and content filters detect harmful text or images in generative apps.

lessons.title: Study plan: hands-on practice for Azure certifications

scenes.text: Suresh, a support engineer in Coimbatore, failed his first administrator exam attempt. He had watched videos for weeks but rarely touched the portal.
For his second attempt he built a lab plan: one hands-on task every day, scenario questions every evening, and a notebook of every mistake.
He passed comfortably — and, more importantly, solved a real networking incident at work the following month using what he had practised.

steps.title: Start from the official skills outline
steps.body: Every exam has an official 'skills measured' outline with weighted domains. Download the current version, turn each bullet into a checklist item, and rate yourself 0–3. Outlines are updated periodically, so re-check before your exam date. This course is independent practice material, not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider.

steps.title: Hands-on beats reading
steps.body:
- Use a free account, credits, or sandbox environments; set a **budget alert** first and delete resources after each lab.
- Do each task three ways where possible: portal, Azure CLI, and a Bicep/ARM template.
- Break things deliberately (wrong NSG rule, missing role) and fix them — troubleshooting scenarios are common.
- Keep a 'mistakes notebook': what you got wrong and the rule you learned.

steps.title: How to answer scenario questions
steps.body:
- Read the **last sentence first** — what is actually being asked?
- Underline constraints: 'minimise cost', 'least administrative effort', 'least privilege', 'no downtime', 'must not use public IPs'.
- Eliminate answers that violate any constraint, even if they would work.
- Prefer managed, built-in features over custom scripts unless the question demands otherwise.
- Watch for qualifiers like 'Standard tier', 'same region', 'P1 licence' — they often decide the answer.

steps.title: Worked example: decoding a question
steps.body:
'You need to ensure that users in the Sales department are automatically added to a group that grants access to the CRM app. The solution must minimise administrative effort.'
- Ask: automatic membership → dynamic group.
- Constraint: minimise effort → not manual assigned groups or scripts.
- Hidden requirement: dynamic groups need Microsoft Entra ID P1+.
Answer: create a dynamic security group with rule user.department -eq 'Sales' (and ensure P1 licensing).

steps.title: A 6-week plan for working professionals
steps.body:
- Week 1: identity and governance labs.
- Week 2: storage labs.
- Week 3: compute and containers.
- Week 4: networking (most people's weakest area — give it extra time).
- Week 5: monitoring and backup; full mock exam.
- Week 6: revise the mistakes notebook; second mock; re-lab weak areas.
45–60 minutes a day beats a 6-hour weekend cram.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your exam date, your three weakest domains, and the first three labs you'll do this week. Put a budget alert on your practice subscription today.

activity.prompt: Your certification preparation checklist.
items: Downloaded the current official skills outline
Rated myself 0–3 on every outline bullet
Set up a practice subscription with a budget alert
Completed at least one lab per domain in the portal
Repeated key labs with Azure CLI or Bicep
Kept a mistakes notebook
Practised scenario questions under time pressure
Scheduled the exam and planned revision weeks

quiz.q: The first document to base your study on is…
options: The official skills-measured outline for the current exam
quiz.why: The official skills-measured outline for the current exam says exactly what is tested, and it changes over time. Start there instead of old notes or random blogs.

quiz.q: In a scenario question, 'minimise administrative effort' usually favours…
quiz.why: 'Minimise administrative effort' usually points to built-in managed features. Custom scripts and manual steps need more work.

quiz.q: Before practising in a paid subscription, you should…
options: Set a budget alert and clean up resources after labs
quiz.why: Set a budget alert and clean up resources after labs, so a forgotten resource doesn't cause a surprise bill.

quiz.q: Why break things deliberately in labs?
options: Troubleshooting skills are tested and needed at work
quiz.why: Breaking things deliberately builds troubleshooting skills, which are tested and needed at work. Fixing errors teaches real understanding.

quiz.q: Which reading tactic helps most with long scenarios?
options: Read the final question first, then note constraints
quiz.why: Read the final question first, then note the constraints. That focuses you on what is asked and the limits it sets.

questions.q: Which service stores secrets, keys and certificates?
questions.why: Azure Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates securely.

questions.q: Which service performs OCR and field extraction from invoices?
questions.why: Document Intelligence performs OCR and field extraction from documents like invoices.

questions.q: Event-driven serverless code on Azure is typically built with…
questions.why: Azure Functions is the serverless, event-driven compute service. ExpressRoute and Bastion are networking services.

questions.q: Which messaging service supports topics with multiple subscriptions and dead-letter queues?
questions.why: Service Bus supports topics with multiple subscriptions and dead-letter queues. Queue Storage and Event Hubs do not offer topics like this.

questions.q: Which AI Search feature combines keyword and vector search?
questions.why: Hybrid search in Azure AI Search combines keyword (full-text) and vector search in one query.

questions.q: A function must run every night at 2 AM. Which trigger?
questions.why: A Timer trigger runs a function on a schedule given as a CRON expression, such as every night at 2 AM.

questions.q: An identity must be shared by three Function Apps and survive if one is deleted. Use…
questions.why: A user-assigned managed identity has its own lifecycle, so it can be shared by three apps and remain if one is deleted. A system-assigned identity is deleted with its resource.

questions.q: Detect personal information in text before storing it — use…
questions.why: The Azure AI Language service has PII detection, which finds personal information in text so it can be redacted before storing.

questions.q: A Cosmos DB container has a 'hot' partition. Most likely design issue?
options: A low-cardinality or skewed partition key
questions.why: A hot partition usually comes from a low-cardinality or skewed partition key that sends most requests to one partition. Choose an evenly distributed, high-cardinality key.

questions.q: Public APIs need rate limiting, key/token validation and a developer portal. Use…
questions.why: API Management provides rate limiting, key and token validation, and a developer portal for public APIs.

questions.q: A RAG assistant on Azure needs grounded answers over 200,000 PDFs with access control. A suitable design is…
options: Azure OpenAI alone with all PDFs pasted into the prompt
AI Search index with security filtering + Azure OpenAI generating answers with citations
questions.why: For a RAG assistant over many PDFs with access control, use an AI Search index with security filtering and have Azure OpenAI generate answers with citations. Pasting 200,000 PDFs into a prompt is impossible.

questions.q: Scenario question says: 'solution must not store any credentials in code or configuration'. Which answer pattern fits?
options: Managed identity + RBAC on the target resource
questions.why: 'No credentials in code or configuration' points to a managed identity with RBAC on the target resource. Connection strings and keys are credentials.

tech-codelab-samples.title: Code Lab samples
tech-codelab-samples.description: Six hands-on coding lessons that run in your browser: real Python, JavaScript, SQLite and HTML/CSS, a simulated Express server and a Java teaching interpreter.

courses.title: Run real code: Python, JavaScript & SQL
courses.summary: Write and run real programs in your browser: Python with input and f-strings, JavaScript array methods and SQL queries on a real SQLite database — each checked by automatic tests.
outcomes: Learners can read input and print formatted output in Python
Learners can use filter, Math.max and reduce on JavaScript arrays
Learners can filter and sort rows with SQL WHERE, AND and ORDER BY
Learners can read a test diff to find the first character that differs

lessons.title: Python: input, maths and f-strings

scenes.text: Asha wants a tiny program that greets her friends and tells them how old they turn this year.
Her friends type their name and birth year. The program reads both with input().
One subtraction and one f-string later, everyone gets a cheerful personal message.

steps.title: input() always gives you text
steps.body:
`input()` reads one line that the user typed and returns it as a **string** (text).

If you need a number, convert it: `year = int(input())`. Without `int(...)`, `"2010" - 1` is an error, because you cannot subtract from text.

steps.title: Worked example: age this year
steps.body:
- Read: `name = input()` → "Asha"
- Read: `year = int(input())` → 2010
- Compute: `age = 2026 - year` → 16
- Print: `print(f"You turn {age} in 2026.")`

An **f-string** starts with `f` and puts any variable inside `{ }` straight into the text.

steps.title: Print exactly what is asked
steps.body: Automatic tests compare your output **character by character**. A missing full stop or an extra space makes a test fail — the Code Lab shows you the first character that differs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `int(...)` around `input()`
- Writing `print("Namaste, {name}!")` without the `f` — Python then prints the braces literally
- Typing your own prompt text inside `input("…")` when the task says not to — it becomes part of the output

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body: Finish the program in the Code Lab. Type sample input in the **stdin** box (one value per line), press **Run**, then press **Check** to run all tests.

activity.prompt:
Read a **name** (line 1) and a **birth year** (line 2). Print exactly two lines:
- `Namaste, <name>!`
- `You turn <age> in 2026.`
activity.starter:
name = input()
year = int(input())

# TODO: work out the age they turn in 2026
# TODO: print "Namaste, <name>!" and "You turn <age> in 2026."
activity.solution:
name = input()
year = int(input())
age = 2026 - year
print(f"Namaste, {name}!")
print(f"You turn {age} in 2026.")
activity.hint: `age = 2026 - year`, then use two `print(f"…")` lines. Check the full stop at the end of the second line!

quiz.q: What type of value does input() return?
options: It depends on what you type
quiz.why: input() always returns text; convert with int() or float() when you need a number.

quiz.q: Which line prints Hi Asha when name = 'Asha'?
quiz.why: Only an f-string replaces {name} with the variable's value: print(f'Hi {name}'). Without the f, the braces are printed literally, and print(Hi name) is a syntax error.

quiz.q: year = input() and the user types 2010. What does 2026 - year do?
quiz.why: input() always returns a string, so 2026 − year tries to subtract text from a number, which raises a TypeError. Convert first with int(input()).

quiz.q: Why might a test fail even though your answer 'looks right'?
options: Spacing or punctuation differs from the expected output
quiz.why: Tests compare text exactly; the diff view shows the first character that differs.

lessons.title: JavaScript arrays: filter, Math.max and averages

scenes.text: Ravi's teacher has a line of marks and wants three quick facts before the parent meeting.
How many passed? What is the top score? What is the class average?
Ravi writes six lines of JavaScript instead of a spreadsheet — and it works for any class size.

steps.title: Arrays hold many values
steps.body:
`const marks = [45, 82, 67];` stores three numbers in order. `marks.length` is 3.

In this lab, `prompt()` reads one line from the **stdin** box, so `prompt().split(" ").map(Number)` turns "45 82 67" into `[45, 82, 67]`.

steps.title: Three tools you will use
steps.body:
- `marks.filter(m => m >= 40)` → a new array with only the passes
- `Math.max(...marks)` → the largest number (the `...` spreads the array into separate arguments)
- `marks.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` → the total; divide by `marks.length` for the average

steps.title: One decimal place
steps.body: `(66).toFixed(1)` gives the text "66.0" and `(53.3333).toFixed(1)` gives "53.3". `toFixed` rounds and always shows the number of decimals you ask for.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `Math.max(marks)` (without `...`) gives `NaN`
- Forgetting the starting value `0` in `reduce` on an empty array
- Dividing by the number of *passes* instead of *all* marks

steps.title: Where this shows up
steps.body: Dashboards, fitness apps and online shops all filter, find maximums and average lists of numbers — usually with exactly these array methods.

activity.prompt:
The input is **one line of marks** separated by spaces. Print exactly:
- `Passed: <how many are 40 or more>`
- `Top score: <highest mark>`
- `Average: <average of all marks, 1 decimal>`
activity.hint: `Math.max(...marks)` for the top score. For the average: `marks.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / marks.length`, then `.toFixed(1)`.

quiz.q: What does [3, 8, 1].filter(x => x > 2) return?
quiz.why: filter keeps the elements for which the test is true. 3 and 8 are greater than 2, so the result is [3, 8].

quiz.q: Math.max(...[4, 9, 2]) gives…
quiz.why: The spread operator ... passes the array's items as separate arguments, so Math.max(4, 9, 2) gives 9.

quiz.q: What does (7).toFixed(1) produce?
quiz.why: toFixed returns a string with exactly the requested number of decimals, so (7).toFixed(1) is "7.0", not the number 7.
reduce starts at 0 and adds each element: 0 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 12.

sources: MDN Web Docs: Array.prototype.filter, Math.max, Array.prototype.reduce

lessons.title: SQL: WHERE, AND and ORDER BY on real SQLite

scenes.text: The Pune centre wants to invite its strongest students to a weekend science camp.
All students from every city live in one table called students.
Meera writes one SQL query that keeps only Pune students above 80 marks, best first.

steps.title: A query has a fixed shape
steps.body:
`SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY column;`

- **SELECT** picks the columns
- **WHERE** keeps only matching rows
- **ORDER BY … DESC** sorts from highest to lowest

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
`SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = 'Delhi';` gives Ravi and Zoya.

Combine conditions with **AND**: `WHERE city = 'Delhi' AND marks > 80` gives only Zoya.

steps.title: Text needs quotes
steps.body: Write text values in single quotes: `'Pune'`. Numbers need no quotes: `marks > 80`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `WHERE city = Pune` (no quotes) → SQLite looks for a *column* called Pune
- Putting `ORDER BY` before `WHERE`
- Using `>=` when the task says *above* 80

steps.title: This is real SQLite
steps.body: The Code Lab runs SQLite compiled to WebAssembly. A fresh database is built from the setup script every time you press Run, so you cannot break anything.

activity.prompt: Show the **name** and **marks** of students from **Pune** with marks **above 80**, highest marks first.
activity.starter:
SELECT name, marks
FROM students
-- TODO: only Pune, marks above 80, highest first
;
activity.solution:
SELECT name, marks
FROM students
WHERE city = 'Pune' AND marks > 80
ORDER BY marks DESC;
activity.hint: You need `WHERE city = 'Pune' AND marks > 80` and then `ORDER BY marks DESC`.

quiz.q: Which clause keeps only some rows?
quiz.why: WHERE filters rows by a condition. SELECT chooses columns, and ORDER BY sorts.

quiz.q: How do you sort from highest to lowest marks?
quiz.why: ORDER BY marks DESC sorts from the highest to the lowest. Without DESC, ORDER BY sorts lowest first.

quiz.q: What is wrong with WHERE city = Pune?
quiz.why: Text values in SQL need quotes. Without them, Pune is read as a column name, so write WHERE city = 'Pune'. SQL uses a single = for comparison.

quiz.q: marks > 80 AND city = 'Pune' keeps a row when…
quiz.why: AND needs both conditions to be true. A row stays only if marks > 80 and city = 'Pune' together.

questions.q: Which Python line converts typed text to a whole number?
questions.why: input() returns text, and int() converts it to a whole number: int(input()).

questions.q: What does print(f'{2+3} apples') show?
questions.why: Expressions inside the braces of an f-string are evaluated, so {2+3} becomes 5 and the output is '5 apples'.

questions.q: In JavaScript, [1,2,3].filter(x => x !== 2) gives…
questions.why: filter keeps the elements for which the test is true. Removing 2 leaves [1, 3].

questions.q: Which SQL clause sorts results?
questions.why: ORDER BY sorts the results. Add DESC to put the highest first.

questions.q: A test expects 'Average: 66.0' and you print 'Average: 66'. What fixes it in JavaScript?
questions.why: toFixed(1) always shows one decimal place, so 66 becomes "66.0". The others drop or round the decimal part.

questions.q: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80 AND city = 'Delhi'; with Ravi(Delhi,78) and Zoya(Delhi,94) returns…
questions.why: Both conditions must hold: marks > 80 and city = 'Delhi'. Ravi has 78, which fails, so only Zoya (94) is returned.

questions.q: Python: year = input(); age = 2026 - year. What happens?
questions.why: input() gives a string, so 2026 − year subtracts a string from an integer, which raises a TypeError. Convert with int().

questions.q: Math.max(...[]) in JavaScript returns…
questions.why: Math.max with no arguments returns -Infinity, since there is no number to compare. Check for empty arrays before using it.

questions.q: Which query counts students per city?
options: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city;
SELECT city FROM students ORDER BY COUNT;
questions.why: GROUP BY city makes one row per city, and COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group. The other forms aren't valid or don't give counts per city.

questions.q: (0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2) in JavaScript gives…
questions.why: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 because of floating-point error. toFixed(2) rounds it and returns the string "0.30".

questions.q: In SQL, which condition finds names starting with A?
questions.why: LIKE with the % wildcard matches any characters, so name LIKE 'A%' finds names that start with A. '=' would look for the literal text 'A%'.

questions.q: The Code Lab's Python runs on…
options: Pyodide (CPython compiled to WebAssembly) in your browser
questions.why: The Code Lab runs Python with Pyodide, which is real CPython compiled to WebAssembly. It runs in a sandboxed worker in your browser, with no remote server.

courses.title: Web pages, servers & Java
courses.summary: Build a web page with HTML and CSS, write your first Express API in a simulated server, and practise Java methods and loops on an educational interpreter.
outcomes: Learners can structure a page with headings and lists and style it with CSS
Learners can write Express routes with parameters, JSON replies and status codes
Learners can write a Java method with a while loop and integer arithmetic
Learners can explain what runs their code: real runtime, simulation or teaching interpreter

lessons.title: HTML & CSS: a study-plan page

scenes.text: Zoya wants a tiny web page on her phone that shows today's study plan.
HTML gives the page its structure: a heading, a list and a button.
One line of CSS gives the heading her favourite deep-teal colour.

steps.title: Tags build the page
steps.body:
- `

…

` is the main heading - `
    ` starts a bullet list and each item is `
  • …
    • ` - `

steps.title: CSS colours an element
steps.body: Inside `<style>` write `h1 { color: #1d5c63; }`. The part before `{` (the **selector**) chooses which elements; inside the braces go **property: value;** pairs.

steps.title: Watch the live preview
steps.body: The preview re-draws as you type. Use 📱 to see your page at phone width (360 px).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to close a tag, e.g. `
  • Maths` without `
    • ` - Missing `;` or `}` in CSS, so later rules are ignored - Writing `colour` (British spelling) — CSS only understands `color`

steps.title: Every website starts here
steps.body: From news sites to banking apps, the browser always receives HTML for structure and CSS for looks.

activity.prompt:
Complete the page:
- an `<h1>` that says **My Study Plan**
- a `<ul>` list with **Maths**, **Science**, **English** (in that order)
- CSS that makes the `h1` colour **#1d5c63**
activity.solution:
My Study Plan

  • Maths
  • Science
  • English
activity.hint:
Add `

My Study Plan

`, then `
  • Maths
  • Science
  • English
`, and in the style block `h1 { color: #1d5c63; }`.

quiz.q: Which tag makes one item of a bullet list?
quiz.why: <ul> makes the bullet list, and each item inside it is an <li> (list item).

quiz.q: In h1 { color: red; } what is h1?
quiz.why: In a CSS rule, the part before the braces is the selector. It chooses which elements the rule styles; here h1 elements.

quiz.q: Why might a CSS rule after a broken one be ignored?
options: Browsers only read the first rule
A missing } or ; confuses the parser
quiz.why: A missing } or ; confuses the parser, which can swallow the rules that follow. That is why a rule after a broken one may be ignored.

quiz.q: Which is the correct CSS property name?
quiz.why: CSS uses the American spelling, so the property is color. 'colour' is not valid.

sources: MDN Web Docs: HTML elements, CSS color

lessons.title: Node.js + Express: your first API (simulated server)

scenes.text: Kabir's friend is building a quiz app and needs a server that squares numbers.
Kabir writes an Express route: when the app asks for /api/square/7 it answers with JSON.
He tests it with a fake HTTP client — the server runs entirely inside his browser tab.

steps.title: Routes connect URLs to code
steps.body:
`app.get("/hello", (req, res) => res.send("Hi"));` means: when a **GET** request for **/hello** arrives, run this function and send back "Hi".

`req` is the incoming request; `res` is how you reply.

steps.title: Route parameters
steps.body: In `app.get("/api/square/:n", …)` the `:n` part is a **parameter**. For /api/square/7, `req.params.n` is the text "7" — convert it with `Number(req.params.n)`.

steps.title: Replying with JSON and a status
steps.body:
- `res.json({ n: 7, square: 49 })` sends `{"n":7,"square":49}`
- `res.status(400).json({ error: "n must be a number" })` signals a bad request
- Use `return` so the function stops after replying

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `app.listen(3000)` — no server, no answers
- Sending two responses for one request ("Cannot set headers after they are sent")
- Treating `req.params.n` as a number without converting it

steps.title: Honest note: simulated
steps.body: This lab is **not real Node.js**. Your JavaScript runs in a browser sandbox with a small built-in `express` shim and a fake HTTP client, so the ideas and code shape match real Express.

activity.prompt: Add a route **GET /api/square/:n** that replies with JSON `{"n": <n>, "square": <n×n>}`. If `n` is not a number, reply with status **400** and `{"error": "n must be a number"}`. Press **Run**, then try the quick requests in the fake HTTP client.
activity.hint: Inside the route: `const n = Number(req.params.n);` then `if (Number.isNaN(n)) return res.status(400).json({ error: "n must be a number" });` and finally `res.json({ n: n, square: n * n });`

quiz.q: In app.get('/user/:id', …), how do you read the id?
quiz.why: In Express, route parameters like :id are available in req.params, so read it as req.params.id. Query-string values are in req.query.

quiz.q: What does res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' }) do?
options: Sends a 404 status with a JSON body
quiz.why: res.status(404) sets the status code and .json(...) sends the object as a JSON body. So it sends a 404 with a JSON body.

quiz.q: Your server never answers any request. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.why: If the server never answers, app.listen(...) was probably missing. Without it, the server never starts listening for requests.

quiz.q: req.params.n for /api/square/7 is…
quiz.why: URL parts arrive as text, so req.params.n is the string "7". Convert with Number() before doing maths.

lessons.title: Java basics: Scanner, loops and methods

scenes.text: Ishan's cousin believes a number is lucky when its digits add up to a big total.
Ishan writes a Java method that peels off digits one at a time with % 10 and / 10.
He tests it on 4096, 7 and 100200 before showing his cousin.

steps.title: Every Java program has main
steps.body:
Java code lives in a class. The program starts at `public static void main(String[] args)`.

`Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);` reads input; `sc.nextInt()` reads the next whole number.

steps.title: Peeling digits with % and /
steps.body:
For n = 4096:
- `n % 10` → 6 (last digit), then `n = n / 10` → 409
- 9, then 40
- 0, then 4
- 4, then 0 → stop

Sum = 6 + 9 + 0 + 4 = **19**. Integer division `/` drops the decimals.

steps.title: Methods return answers
steps.body: `static int sumDigits(int n) { … return sum; }` takes an int and gives one back. Call it from main: `sumDigits(4096)`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing `while (n > 0)` but forgetting `n = n / 10;` → an infinite loop (the Code Lab stops it for you)
- Returning `sum` before the loop finishes
- Using `String` + `int` without a space: `"Sum:" + 19` prints `Sum:19`

steps.title: Honest note: educational interpreter
steps.body: This lab runs Java on VidyaVerse's **educational interpreter for a subset of Java** (variables, loops, methods, arrays, String, Scanner, collections) — not a full JVM. Real Java compilers may catch some mistakes earlier.

activity.prompt: Complete `sumDigits` so it returns the **sum of the digits** of `n`. The program reads `n` and prints `Digits: <count>` and `Sum: <sum>`.
activity.hint: Use `while (n > 0) { sum += n % 10; n = n / 10; }` before `return sum;`.

quiz.q: What is 4096 % 10 in Java?
quiz.why: The % operator gives the remainder after division. 4096 % 10 = 6, which is the last digit.

quiz.q: What is 4096 / 10 when both are int?
quiz.why: With two int values, Java does integer division and drops the decimal part. 4096 / 10 is 409, not 409.6.

quiz.q: Where does a Java program start running?
quiz.why: A Java program starts at the main method: public static void main(String[] args).

quiz.q: while (n > 0) { sum += n % 10; } never ends. Why?
quiz.why: The loop condition n > 0 stays true if n never changes. Add n = n / 10 inside the loop so it moves towards false.

questions.q: Which tag is the main heading of a page?
questions.why: <h1> is the main heading displayed on the page. <title> sets the text in the browser tab.

questions.q: Which CSS rule colours every paragraph blue?
questions.why: A CSS rule is written selector { property: value; }, so p { color: blue; } makes every paragraph blue.

questions.q: In Express, what does res.json({ ok: true }) send?
questions.why: res.json({ ok: true }) turns the object into JSON and sends {"ok":true} as the response.

questions.q: Which Express route matches /api/books/42?
questions.why: The route /api/books/:id uses :id as a parameter, so it matches /api/books/42. The method must also be GET to match a GET request.

questions.q: Java: int x = 7 / 2; System.out.println(x); prints…
questions.why: In Java, int x = 7 / 2 is integer division, so the decimal part is dropped and x is 3.

questions.q: Java: double d = 7 / 2; System.out.println(d); prints…
questions.why: 7 / 2 is computed as integer division first, giving 3, and then stored in the double as 3.0. Write 7 / 2.0 to get 3.5.

questions.q: A route must reject bad input. Which status code fits 'the client sent something invalid'?
questions.why: 400 means Bad Request: the client sent something invalid. 500 means the server itself failed.

questions.q: Why does Express print 'Cannot set headers after they are sent'?
questions.why: That error means the route sent a response twice. Each request gets exactly one response, so use return after replying.

questions.q: Java: what does "Sum: " + 1 + 2 print?
questions.why: Java evaluates left to right. "Sum: " + 1 becomes the text "Sum: 1", and then + 2 appends "2", giving "Sum: 12". Use brackets (1 + 2) to add first.

questions.q: In CSS, which selector targets the element with id="msg"?
questions.why: In CSS, # selects an element by its id and . selects by class. So #msg targets id="msg".

questions.q: A Java while loop never ends. What is the most common cause?
questions.why: A while loop that never ends usually has a loop variable that never changes. If nothing moves the condition towards false, it repeats forever.

questions.q: The Code Lab's Node.js/Express lab is best described as…
options: Real Node.js on a cloud server
A simulated server running in your browser with an express shim
questions.why: The Node.js/Express lab is a simulated server running in your browser, using an express shim. The code looks like real Express, but it doesn't run on a cloud server.

tech-data-systems.title: Data, SQL and systems design
tech-data-systems.description: Query data with SQL from zero to window functions, build reliable data pipelines, and design scalable distributed systems — including how to handle system design interviews.

courses.title: SQL from zero to confident
courses.summary: Learn SQL step by step with one running example — a school canteen and a small online shop: selecting and filtering, aggregating, joining tables, subqueries, CTEs and window functions, then designing tables with keys, normalisation, indexes and transactions.
outcomes: Learners can write SELECT queries with filters, sorting and limits, and handle NULL correctly
Learners can aggregate with GROUP BY and HAVING
Learners can combine tables with INNER, LEFT and other joins
Learners can use subqueries, CTEs and window functions for ranking and running totals
Learners can design normalised tables with keys and indexes and explain ACID transactions

lessons.title: Tables, SELECT and WHERE

scenes.text: Kamala aunty runs the canteen at a school in Thrissur. Her son Jijo, a Class 12 student, moved her sales notebook into a database table called sales.
She asked: 'Which items sold more than 50 plates on Monday?' Jijo typed one line of SQL and the answer appeared.
'So I can ask the computer questions in nearly-English?' she said. 'Exactly,' said Jijo. 'That's SQL — Structured Query Language.'

steps.title: Tables, rows, columns
steps.body:
A **relational database** stores data in **tables**. Each **row** is one record (one sale); each **column** is one attribute with a data type (item TEXT, qty INTEGER, price NUMERIC, sold_on DATE).
Example table sales:
- (1, 'Idli', 60, 20, '2025-07-07')
- (2, 'Dosa', 45, 35, '2025-07-07')
- (3, 'Idli', 30, 20, '2025-07-08')
SQL works in databases such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server and Oracle; core syntax is very similar across them.

steps.title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT
steps.body:
SELECT item, qty
FROM sales
WHERE sold_on = '2025-07-07' AND qty > 50
ORDER BY qty DESC
LIMIT 5;

- **SELECT** picks columns (SELECT * means all — avoid in real code).
- **WHERE** filters rows: =, <>, <, >, BETWEEN, IN ('Idli', 'Dosa'), LIKE 'D%' (starts with D).
- **ORDER BY** sorts (ASC default, DESC for descending).
- **LIMIT** (or TOP / FETCH FIRST in some databases) restricts row count.
- Computed columns and aliases: SELECT item, qty * price AS revenue.

steps.title: NULL: the missing value
steps.body:
NULL means 'unknown/missing', not zero or empty text.
- WHERE price = NULL never matches — use **WHERE price IS NULL** (or IS NOT NULL).
- Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 5 + NULL = NULL.
- COALESCE(price, 0) replaces NULL with 0 for display or maths.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Question: 'Top 3 items by revenue on 7 July.'
SELECT item, qty * price AS revenue
FROM sales
WHERE sold_on = '2025-07-07'
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;
With the rows above: Dosa 45 × 35 = 1575, Idli 60 × 20 = 1200.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Use any free online SQL playground (SQLite works in the browser). Create the sales table, insert 8 rows, and answer: which items cost more than ₹25? Which sales happened on 8 July? Which rows have no price recorded?

activity.prompt: Complete the query to find sales with missing price, newest first.
activity.text: SELECT * FROM sales WHERE price ___ NULL ORDER BY sold_on ___;

quiz.q: Which clause filters rows?
quiz.why: WHERE filters rows by a condition. SELECT chooses columns, and ORDER BY sorts.
