questions.why: With last-write-wins and unsynchronised clocks, clock skew can make an older update look newer. So a genuinely newer update can be silently discarded.

tech-programming.title: Programming from zero
tech-programming.description: Start coding with no experience: algorithms for children, Python and JavaScript from scratch, then object-oriented design, testing, debugging and Git.

courses.title: Think like a coder (no computer needed to start)
courses.summary: A gentle first step into coding for children: algorithms, sequences, loops, conditions and debugging, practised with the turtle-drawing lab and the code maze game.
outcomes: Learners can write a clear step-by-step algorithm for an everyday task
Learners can spot repeated steps and replace them with a loop
Learners can use if/else to make a program choose
Learners can find and fix a bug by testing one step at a time

lessons.title: Algorithms are recipes

story.title: Anaya makes lemonade for a robot

scenes.text: Anaya in Pune wanted her toy robot Chotu to make lemonade. She said: 'Make lemonade!' Chotu did nothing.
Her brother Kabir laughed: 'Chotu only understands tiny, exact steps. You must tell it EVERYTHING, in the right order.'
Anaya wrote: 1. Take a glass. 2. Squeeze half a lemon into it. 3. Add 2 spoons of sugar. 4. Pour water. 5. Stir 10 times.
When they acted it out, Kabir poured water before taking the glass — splash! Order matters. Anaya had just written her first algorithm.

steps.title: What is an algorithm?
steps.body:
An **algorithm** is a list of steps that solves a problem, written so clearly that anyone (or any machine) following it gets the same result.

You already use algorithms every day:
- brushing your teeth
- tying your shoelaces
- the way you walk to school

A **program** is just an algorithm written in a language a computer understands, such as Python, JavaScript or Scratch blocks.

steps.title: Three rules of a good algorithm
steps.body:
- **Exact:** 'add some sugar' is unclear; 'add 2 spoons of sugar' is exact.
- **In order:** the steps happen one after another, top to bottom. This is called a **sequence**.
- **Finishes:** it must stop. 'Keep stirring' with no end would go on forever.

Computers are very fast but not clever: they do exactly what you say, not what you mean.

steps.title: Worked example: drawing a square
steps.body:
Imagine a turtle on paper holding a pen. It understands only: *forward(steps)* and *turn right(degrees)*.

To draw a square:
- forward 100, right 90
- forward 100, right 90
- forward 100, right 90
- forward 100, right 90

Why 90? A square has 4 corners and the turtle must turn all the way round (360 degrees) by the end: 360 ÷ 4 = 90.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Skipping a step** because it feels obvious to you ('take a glass'). The computer does not know it.
- **Wrong order** — pouring before holding the glass.
- **Vague words** like 'a little', 'nicely', 'soon'. Replace them with numbers.

steps.title: Try this (unplugged)
steps.body: Ask a grown-up or friend to be the 'robot'. Write steps to make them walk from the door to a chair. They must follow your words *exactly* — no guessing! Every time they bump into something, fix your algorithm. Then open the **turtle lab** and draw a square with the 8 steps above.

activity.prompt: Put Anaya's lemonade algorithm in the right order.
items: Take a clean glass
Squeeze half a lemon into the glass
Add 2 spoons of sugar
Pour water until the glass is nearly full
Stir 10 times
Serve the lemonade

quiz.q: What is an algorithm?
options: A clear list of steps that solves a problem
quiz.why: An algorithm is a precise, ordered set of steps. Programs are algorithms written for computers.

quiz.q: Which instruction is most exact?
quiz.why: A number makes an instruction exact, so everyone gets the same result. 'Some' or 'soon' can mean different things to different people.

quiz.q: To draw a square, the turtle turns right by how many degrees at each corner?
quiz.why: A square has 4 equal corners, and the turtle must turn a full 360 degrees in total. So each turn is 360 ÷ 4 = 90 degrees.

quiz.q: Steps that happen one after another in order are called a…
quiz.why: Steps done one after another in order are a sequence. It is the most basic idea in coding.

quiz.q: Why did Chotu do nothing when told 'Make lemonade!'?
quiz.why: Computers cannot fill gaps. Big vague commands must be broken into small exact steps.

lessons.title: Loops: say it once, repeat it many times

scenes.text: Rohan in Chennai wrote the square steps for his turtle: forward, right, forward, right… eight lines.
Then his teacher Ms. Fernandes asked for a star with 5 points, then a shape with 36 sides. 'That is 72 lines!' Rohan groaned.
Ms. Fernandes smiled: 'When you see the same steps again and again, use a loop. Repeat 4 times: forward 100, right 90.'
Rohan's 36-sided shape took just 3 lines. It looked almost like a circle.

steps.title: What is a loop?
steps.body:
A **loop** repeats a group of steps. Instead of writing the same thing many times, you write it once and say how many times to repeat.

In block languages: *repeat 4 [ forward 100, right 90 ]*.
In Python it looks like this:
for i in range(4):
    forward(100)
    right(90)

The indented lines (pushed in with spaces) are the **body** of the loop — the part that repeats.

steps.title: Worked example: any regular shape
steps.body:
For a shape with **n** equal sides, the turtle turns 360 ÷ n degrees at each corner.
- Triangle: repeat 3 [forward 100, right 120]
- Pentagon: repeat 5 [forward 100, right 72]
- Hexagon: repeat 6 [forward 100, right 60]
- 36 sides: repeat 36 [forward 10, right 10] — looks like a circle.

A 5-pointed star is different: repeat 5 [forward 100, right 144]. The turtle goes round **twice** (5 × 144 = 720).

steps.title: Loops are everywhere
steps.body: A washing machine repeats spin cycles. A music app repeats a song. A traffic light repeats green-yellow-red all day. Computers can repeat millions of times per second without getting bored — that is their superpower.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting a step **inside** the loop that should be **outside** (for example, 'pen up' inside the loop stops the drawing).
- Wrong turn angle — check that turns add up to 360 (or 720 for a star).
- A loop that never stops is called an **infinite loop**. Always know when your loop should end.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the turtle lab: draw a triangle, a hexagon and a star using loops. Challenge: put a loop **inside** a loop — repeat 12 [ draw a square, right 30 ] — and see the flower pattern appear.

activity.prompt: Match each shape to the loop that draws it.

quiz.q: Why do programmers use loops?
options: To repeat steps without rewriting them
quiz.why: Loops save writing and make code easier to change: edit once, every repeat changes.

quiz.q: A turtle turns right 72 degrees, 5 times. What shape?
quiz.why: A turn of 72 degrees, 5 times, makes 72 × 5 = 360 degrees. A shape with 5 equal sides is a pentagon.

quiz.q: What is an infinite loop?
options: A loop that runs exactly once
quiz.why: If nothing ever tells the loop to stop, it runs forever and the program freezes.

quiz.q: In Python, how do we show which lines are inside a loop?
options: Put them in a different file
quiz.why: Python uses indentation, usually 4 spaces, to show which lines are inside the loop.

quiz.q: Turn angle for a regular shape with 8 sides?
quiz.why: The turn angle is 360 divided by the number of sides. For 8 sides, 360 ÷ 8 = 45 degrees.

lessons.title: If this, then that: making choices

scenes.text: Meher in Kochi built a tiny program for her school project: a robot that reminds people what to carry.
'If it is raining, say: take an umbrella. Otherwise, say: take sunglasses.'
Her friend Arjun tested it: rain → umbrella. Sun → sunglasses. Then he asked: 'What if it is very cold?' Meher added another choice.
Her robot now made decisions. 'That,' said her teacher, 'is the difference between a list of steps and a smart program.'

steps.title: Conditions
steps.body:
A **condition** is a question with a yes/no (true/false) answer: *Is it raining? Is the score more than 10? Is there a wall ahead?*

An **if** statement runs some steps only when the condition is true. An **else** gives the steps for when it is false.

In Python:
if raining:
    print('Take an umbrella')
else:
    print('Take sunglasses')

steps.title: Worked example: more than two choices
Choices in real machines
steps.body:
- A lift: if a button is pressed on floor 3, go to floor 3.
- A game: if the player touches a coin, add 1 point.
- A phone: if the battery is below 20%, show a warning.
- The code maze: if there is a wall ahead, turn; else move forward.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking in the wrong order: if you test 'temperature < 25' first, a cold day (8) also matches and you never reach the sweater advice.
- Forgetting the **else** case — what should happen when nothing matches?
- Mixing up **=** (store a value) and **==** (compare two values) in Python.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Play the **code maze** game. Before each move, say your condition aloud: 'If there is a wall in front, I turn right; otherwise I go forward.' Count how many moves your rule needs to escape.

a.text: Your maze robot sees a wall straight ahead and an open path on the right. Which rule should it follow?

choices.label: If wall ahead → turn right
choices.feedback: Yes! A condition checks the wall before moving.

choices.label: Always move forward
choices.feedback: Without a condition, the robot crashes into the wall.

b.text: Now the path ahead is open. What should the robot do?

choices.label: Else → move forward
choices.feedback: Right — the else branch handles the open path.

choices.label: Turn right again
choices.feedback: Turning when the path is open wastes moves and can send you in circles.

c.text: Bonk! The robot bumped the wall or spun in a circle. Bugs like this are normal — let's try again with a condition.

choices.label: Try again
choices.feedback: Good — coders learn by testing and fixing.

d.text: The robot escapes the maze using one simple rule: if wall ahead, turn right; else move forward. You wrote a decision-making program!

quiz.q: What does an 'if' statement do?
options: Runs steps only when a condition is true
quiz.why: An 'if' statement runs its steps only when a condition is true. If it is false, those steps are skipped.

quiz.q: A condition always has an answer of…
quiz.why: A condition is a yes/no question, so its answer is always True or False. These are called Boolean values.

quiz.q: temperature = 30. Using Meher's code, what prints?
quiz.why: 30 is not less than 10, and not less than 25, so the else part runs. It prints 'Drink lots of water!'.

quiz.q: In Python, which symbol compares two values?
quiz.why: The symbol == compares two values and asks 'are they equal?'. A single = stores a value in a variable.

quiz.q: What is 'else' for?
quiz.why: 'else' is the 'otherwise' part. It runs when the condition is false.

lessons.title: Bugs and debugging: be a code detective

scenes.text: Kabir wanted his turtle to draw a house: a square with a triangle roof. He got a square… and a roof floating in the sky.
He wanted to delete everything and start again. His grandmother, a retired engineer in Bengaluru, said: 'Wait. Let's be detectives.'
They ran the program one step at a time and watched where the turtle went. After the square, the turtle was facing the wrong way.
One extra 'right 90' fixed it. 'Every programmer in the world has bugs,' said Nani. 'Good programmers find them calmly.'

steps.title: What is a bug?
steps.body:
A **bug** is a mistake in a program that makes it do something you did not want. Fixing it is called **debugging**.

There are three common kinds:
- **Syntax error:** the computer cannot understand the code (a missing bracket, a spelling mistake like 'pirnt').
- **Runtime error:** the program starts but crashes (for example, dividing by zero).
- **Logic error:** the program runs but gives the wrong answer — like Kabir's floating roof. These are the trickiest.

steps.title: The detective method
steps.body:
- **Reproduce:** run it again — does the bug happen every time?
- **Predict:** say what *should* happen at each step.
- **Observe:** run one step at a time, or add print() lines to see values.
- **Find the first surprise:** the bug is near the first step where reality differs from your prediction.
- **Fix one thing, then test again.**

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Goal: add up 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
total = 0
for n in range(5):
    total = total + n
print(total)

This prints **10**, not 15. Detective work: print n inside the loop → we see 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. range(5) starts at 0 and stops *before* 5! Fix: range(1, 6). Now it prints 15.

steps.title: Rubber duck debugging
steps.body: Explain your code, line by line, out loud to a rubber duck (or a toy, or a pet). Saying it slowly often makes you notice the mistake yourself. Professional programmers really do this.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the turtle lab, deliberately add one wrong turn to your square and watch what happens. Then fix it. Breaking things on purpose is a great way to understand them.

activity.prompt: Sort each bug into its type.

items.text: Opening a file that does not exist
The roof drawn in the wrong place

quiz.q: What is debugging?
options: Finding and fixing mistakes in code
quiz.why: Debugging means finding and fixing mistakes (bugs) in code.

quiz.q: The program runs but gives the wrong answer. This is a…
quiz.why: A program that runs but gives the wrong answer has a logic error. It doesn't crash, so the mistake is easy to miss.

quiz.q: What does range(5) give in Python?
quiz.why: range(5) starts at 0 and stops just before 5, so it gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. That is five numbers.

quiz.q: Best first step when you find a bug?
options: Reproduce it and predict each step
quiz.why: First reproduce the bug and predict what each step should do. Then watch what really happens, and fix one thing at a time.

quiz.q: Why explain code to a rubber duck?
options: Explaining slowly helps you spot your own mistake
quiz.why: Explaining your code slowly, step by step, helps you notice the part that does not make sense. The duck does not need to know Python.

questions.q: An algorithm is…
options: A clear ordered list of steps
questions.why: An algorithm is a clear, ordered list of steps to do a job.

questions.q: Which is a loop?
options: if it rains, take an umbrella
questions.why: A loop repeats steps. 'repeat 4 times: forward, turn' repeats the same steps four times.

questions.q: To draw an equilateral triangle the turtle turns…
questions.why: The three turns of a triangle must add up to 360 degrees. So each turn is 360 ÷ 3 = 120 degrees.

questions.q: Which word means 'otherwise' in code?
questions.why: The word 'else' means 'otherwise'. It runs when the 'if' condition is false.

questions.q: A program crashes when dividing by zero. This is a…
questions.why: A program that starts fine and then fails while running, like when dividing by zero, has a runtime error. A syntax error would stop it from starting.

questions.q: for i in range(3): print('Hi') prints Hi how many times?
questions.why: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2, which is three values. So the loop runs 3 times and prints Hi three times.

questions.q: x = 7. if x > 5: print('big') else: print('small'). Output?
questions.why: x is 7, and 7 > 5 is True, so the if part runs and prints 'big'.

questions.q: Which order is correct for the detective method?
questions.why: The detective method is: reproduce the bug, predict what should happen, observe what does happen, then fix one thing.

questions.q: repeat 5 [forward 100, right 144] draws a…
questions.why: Turning 144 degrees 5 times gives 720 degrees, which is two full turns. The turtle goes round twice and draws a five-point star.

questions.q: total=0; for n in range(1,4): total=total+n. Final total?
questions.why: The loop adds 1, then 2, then 3 to total: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. range(1,4) stops before 4.

questions.q: temperature = 10 with the rules: if <10 sweater; elif <25 T-shirt; else water. Output?
questions.why: 10 is not less than 10, so the first rule fails. 10 is less than 25, so the second rule runs and gives T-shirt.

questions.q: repeat 12 [draw a square, right 30] — how far has the turtle turned in total from the 'right 30' steps?
questions.why: Each 'right 30' turns 30 degrees, and 12 × 30 = 360. That's one full turn, which makes a symmetrical flower pattern.

courses.title: Python from zero
courses.summary: Learn real Python from absolute zero: values and variables, decisions and loops, functions, lists and dictionaries, and handling errors — with worked examples you can type and run.
outcomes: Learners can store and convert data with variables and types
Learners can write programs that decide and repeat
Learners can design reusable functions with parameters and return values
Learners can organise data in lists and dictionaries
Learners can read errors, handle exceptions and build a small project

lessons.title: Values, variables and types

scenes.text: Priya runs a chai stall outside a Hyderabad metro station. Each evening she adds up cups sold on a paper slip — and often gets it wrong when tired.
Her nephew Sameer, a Class 10 student, said: 'Let's make Python do the maths.' He typed: cups = 140 and price = 15.
Then: total = cups * price, and print(total). The screen showed 2100. Priya laughed: 'So the computer just remembers numbers in named boxes?'
'Exactly,' said Sameer. 'Those boxes are called variables.'

steps.title: Your first program
steps.body:
Python runs your file from top to bottom, one line at a time.
print('Namaste, world!')

**print()** shows something on screen. The text inside quotes is a **string** (a piece of text). You can use single or double quotes, but they must match.

To run Python you can install it from python.org and use IDLE, or use any free online Python editor. Type each example yourself — typing builds memory far better than reading.

steps.title: Variables
steps.body:
A **variable** is a name that refers to a value.
cups = 140
price = 15
total = cups * price
print(total)   # 2100

- The **=** sign means *store the right side under the name on the left* — it is not maths equality.
- Names may use letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive (Total and total are different).
- Choose meaningful names: cups_sold beats x.
- Anything after # is a **comment** for humans; Python ignores it.

steps.title: The four basic types
steps.body:
- **int** — whole numbers: 140, -3
- **float** — decimals: 15.5, 0.1
- **str** — text: 'chai', '140'
- **bool** — True or False

Use type(x) to check. Arithmetic: + - * / (always gives a float: 7 / 2 = 3.5), // (floor division: 7 // 2 = 3), % (remainder: 7 % 2 = 1), ** (power: 2 ** 3 = 8).

steps.title: Worked example: input and conversion
steps.body:
input() always returns a **string**, even if the user types a number.
cups = input('Cups sold? ')      # user types 140 → '140'
price = 15
print(cups * price)               # surprise!

'140' * 15 repeats the text 15 times! Convert first:
cups = int(input('Cups sold? '))
print(cups * price)               # 2100

To combine text and numbers neatly, use an **f-string**:
print(f'Today: {cups} cups, Rs {cups * price}')

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting int() or float() around input().
- 'Total: ' + 2100 → TypeError (cannot add str and int). Use an f-string or str(2100).
- Using a variable before giving it a value → NameError.
- Expecting 0.1 + 0.2 to be exactly 0.3 — floats are stored in binary, so you get 0.30000000000000004. For money, round(x, 2) when displaying, or count in paise as integers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a program that asks for a temperature in Celsius and prints it in Fahrenheit. Formula: F = C × 9 / 5 + 32. Test with 100 (should print 212.0) and 37 (about 98.6 — round() tidies tiny float errors).

activity.prompt: Fill in the Python so the program works.

quiz.q: What does cups = 140 do?
quiz.why: A single = is assignment: it stores 140 under the name cups. To compare values you use ==.

quiz.q: Type of the value returned by input()?
quiz.why: input() always returns text (a str). To do maths on it you must convert it with int() or float().

quiz.q: What is 17 // 5 and 17 % 5?
quiz.why: 17 // 5 is floor division, so 3 (5 × 3 = 15). 17 % 5 is the remainder, 17 − 15 = 2.

quiz.q: Which variable name is NOT allowed?
quiz.why: Variable names cannot start with a digit, so 2nd_day is not allowed. Letters, digits and underscores are fine if the name doesn't start with a digit.

quiz.q: '5' + '5' in Python gives…
quiz.why: With strings, + joins (concatenates) the text. So '5' + '5' is '55', not 10.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops

scenes.text: Fatima teaches Class 9 in Lucknow. Every term she converts 40 students' marks into grades by hand.
Her former student Dev, now in college, offered: 'A loop can go through every mark, and if/elif can choose the grade.'
In fifteen lines they had a program that printed every grade and the class average.
Fatima used the saved hour to plan a better lesson.

steps.title: Comparisons and logic
for loops
steps.body:
A **for** loop takes each item from a sequence in turn.
marks = [88, 92, 45, 30]
for m in marks:
    print(m)

**range()** produces numbers: range(5) → 0..4; range(1, 11) → 1..10; range(0, 20, 5) → 0, 5, 10, 15.

steps.title: while loops, break and continue
steps.body:
A **while** loop repeats as long as a condition is True — useful when you do not know the count in advance.
pin = ''
while pin != '4321':
    pin = input('PIN: ')
print('Welcome')

- **break** leaves the loop immediately.
- **continue** skips to the next repetition.
Always make sure something inside the loop eventually makes the condition False.

steps.title: Worked example: class average and topper
steps.body:
marks = [88, 92, 45, 30, 76]
total = 0
best = marks[0]
for m in marks:
    total += m           # same as total = total + m
    if m > best:
        best = m
avg = total / len(marks)
print(f'Average {avg:.1f}, highest {best}')

Output: Average 66.2, highest 92. (Python also has sum(marks) and max(marks), but writing it yourself teaches the **accumulator pattern** used everywhere.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Order of elif matters: test the highest range first, or 95 might be graded 'Pass'.
- **Off-by-one:** range(1, 10) stops at 9.
- Infinite while loop: forgetting to update the variable the condition depends on.
- Using = instead of == inside if → SyntaxError.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: FizzBuzz, a classic interview warm-up: print numbers 1 to 30, but print 'Fizz' for multiples of 3, 'Buzz' for multiples of 5, and 'FizzBuzz' for multiples of both. Hint: check the 'both' case (n % 15 == 0) first.

statements.s: range(1, 5) produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
statements.why: range stops before the end value: 1, 2, 3, 4.

statements.s: A while loop may run zero times.
statements.why: If the condition is False at the start, the body never runs.

statements.s: break skips only the current repetition.
statements.why: That is continue; break exits the whole loop.

statements.s: In if/elif/else, more than one branch can run.
statements.why: Only the first true branch runs.

statements.s: not (5 > 3) is False.
statements.why: 5 > 3 is True; not True is False.

quiz.q: marks = 80. With the grading code (>=90 A1, >=75 A2, >=33 Pass), the grade is…
quiz.why: 80 is not >= 90, so the first test fails. It passes >= 75, so the grade is A2.

quiz.q: How many numbers does range(0, 20, 5) produce?
quiz.why: range(0, 20, 5) starts at 0 and steps by 5 until before 20: 0, 5, 10, 15. That is 4 numbers.

quiz.q: Which loop is best when you do not know how many times to repeat?
quiz.why: A while loop repeats until a condition changes, so it fits when you don't know the number of repeats. A for loop with range needs a known count.

quiz.q: For FizzBuzz, why check n % 15 == 0 first?
options: Otherwise multiples of 15 would match the 3-check first and print only Fizz
quiz.why: A multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 3. If you check 3 first, it matches and prints only Fizz. Check the specific case (15) first.

quiz.q: total += m means…
quiz.why: total += m is shorthand for total = total + m. It adds m to the existing value.

lessons.title: Functions: name a job, reuse it

scenes.text: Arjun runs a small electronics shop in Jaipur. He kept copying the same three lines to add GST to every bill.
When he changed the formula, he forgot one copy — and undercharged a customer for a week.
His friend Neha, a developer, rewrote it as one function: add_tax(amount, rate). Every bill now called the same function.
'Change it in one place, fixed everywhere,' Neha said. 'That's the point of functions.'

steps.title: Defining and calling a function
steps.body:
A **function** is a named, reusable block of code.
def add_tax(amount, rate):
    tax = amount * rate / 100
    return amount + tax

bill = add_tax(1000, 18)
print(bill)   # 1180.0

- **def** starts the definition; amount and rate are **parameters**.
- 1000 and 18 are **arguments** — the actual values passed in.
- **return** sends a value back to the caller and ends the function.

steps.title: Defaults, keywords and scope
Worked example: break a problem into functions
print vs return — the #1 beginner confusion
steps.body:
def double(x):
    print(x * 2)
result = double(5)    # shows 10
print(result)         # None!

print only *shows* a value; return *gives it back* so other code can use it. A function without return gives back **None**. Also: writing double instead of double(5) refers to the function itself without running it.

steps.title: Good function habits
steps.body:
- Name functions with verbs: calculate_total, send_email.
- Keep them short (often under 20 lines).
- Write a docstring (a triple-quoted sentence) as the first line, saying what the function returns.
- Test with simple known answers first (100 at 18% → 118).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write bmi(weight_kg, height_m) that returns weight ÷ height². Then write category(b) returning 'under' if b < 18.5, 'normal' if b < 25, else 'over'. (These are the general WHO adult cut-offs; BMI is a rough screening number, not a diagnosis.)

activity.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Name in the definition that receives a value
Sends a result back to the caller
What a function gives back with no return

quiz.q: def f(x): return x + 1. What is f(f(2))?
A function with no return statement returns…
quiz.why: A function with no return statement returns None by default.

quiz.q: Is 1900 a leap year by the Gregorian rule?
quiz.why: 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it is not a leap year in the Gregorian rule.

quiz.q: Main benefit of functions?
options: Reuse and change logic in one place
quiz.why: Functions let you reuse code and change the logic in one place. Arjun's bug came from code that was copied in several places.

quiz.q: add_tax(500, rate=5) with def add_tax(amount, rate=18) returns about…
quiz.why: With rate = 5, the function adds 5% tax: 500 × 1.05 = 525. The default of 18 is used only if no rate is given.

lessons.title: Lists and dictionaries

scenes.text: Grace volunteers at a community library in Shillong. The book register is a tattered notebook.
Her cousin Tenzin showed her a Python list for the shelf of titles, and a dictionary linking each title to who borrowed it.
Finding who had 'Wings of Fire' became one line: borrowed['Wings of Fire'].
Grace said: 'Lists are like a queue; dictionaries are like a phone book.' Tenzin grinned: 'Perfect description.'

steps.title: Lists: ordered collections
steps.body:
books = ['Malgudi Days', 'Wings of Fire', 'Gitanjali']
- Index from 0: books[0] is 'Malgudi Days'; books[-1] is the last item.
- books.append('Godaan') adds to the end; books.remove('Gitanjali') removes by value; len(books) counts.
- **Slicing:** books[0:2] gives the first two items.
- Lists are **mutable** — you can change them: books[1] = 'Ignited Minds'.
- 'Godaan' in books → True or False.

steps.title: Dictionaries: key → value
steps.body:
borrowed = {'Wings of Fire': 'Tenzin', 'Godaan': 'Ri'}
borrowed['Gitanjali'] = 'Grace'    # add or update
print(borrowed['Godaan'])          # Ri
print(borrowed.get('Malgudi Days', 'on shelf'))  # safe lookup
for title, person in borrowed.items():
    print(title, '→', person)

Keys must be unique and immutable (strings, numbers, tuples). Looking up a key in a dictionary is very fast, even with millions of entries.

steps.title: Worked example: counting words
Also useful: tuples, sets, comprehensions
steps.body:
- **tuple:** ('Pune', 18.5) — like a list but cannot be changed; good for fixed records.
- **set:** {'red', 'blue'} — unique items, no order; great for removing duplicates: set(names).
- **List comprehension:** squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)] → [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]. With a filter: [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- books[3] on a 3-item list → IndexError (indexes are 0, 1, 2).
- borrowed['Unknown'] → KeyError; use .get() when the key might be missing.
- b = books does NOT copy — both names point to the same list. Use books.copy().
- Changing a list while looping over it causes skipped items; loop over a copy.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a dictionary of 5 friends' names → birth months. Write code that prints everyone born in a month you ask for with input(). Then use a set to print the distinct months.

activity.prompt: Which data structure fits best?

items.text: Songs in a playlist, in play order

quiz.why: A negative index counts from the end of the list. nums[-1] is the last item, 30.

quiz.q: Safe dictionary lookup that avoids KeyError?
quiz.why: d.get(k, default) returns the default value if the key is missing. d[k] raises a KeyError instead.

quiz.q: [n * 2 for n in range(3)] gives…
quiz.why: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 and each is doubled: [0, 2, 4].
A set keeps only unique items. ['a', 'b', 'a', 'c'] has three different values, so len is 3.

quiz.q: b = books; b.append('X'). What happens to books?
quiz.why: b = books does not copy the list. Both names refer to the same list object, so appending through b also changes books.

lessons.title: Errors, exceptions and a mini project

scenes.text: Ravi, a first-year B.Com student in Kolkata, wanted to track his monthly spending on food, travel and mobile recharge.
His first version crashed whenever he typed 'fifty' instead of 50: ValueError: invalid literal for int().
He learned try/except, so the program politely asked again instead of crashing, and saved data to a file so nothing was lost overnight.
At month-end it printed totals by category. He discovered he spent more on snacks than on books.

steps.title: Reading a traceback
steps.body:
When Python crashes it prints a **traceback**. Read it from the **bottom**:
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fifty'
- The last line names the **error type** and message.
- Lines above show the file, line number and code that failed.
Common types: SyntaxError, NameError (unknown name), TypeError (wrong type), ValueError (right type, bad value), IndexError, KeyError, ZeroDivisionError, FileNotFoundError.

steps.title: try / except
Files
steps.body:
with open('expenses.csv', 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write(f'{category},{amount}\n')

- Modes: 'r' read, 'w' write (erases!), 'a' append.
- **with** closes the file automatically, even after an error.
- Reading: for line in open('expenses.csv', encoding='utf-8'): cat, amt = line.strip().split(',')

steps.title: Worked example: totals by category
Project habits that professionals use
steps.body:
- Start tiny: make one feature work, then add the next.
- Keep data separate from code (the CSV file).
- Test strange input: empty lines, negative numbers, text.
- Use **virtual environments** (python -m venv .venv) when you start installing packages with pip, so projects do not clash.
- Put your project under Git (see the Git lesson).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Build Ravi's tracker: a menu loop with options 1) add expense 2) show totals 3) quit. Handle bad input with try/except. Bonus: warn when any category passes a budget you set in a dictionary.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for adding one expense safely.
items: Show the menu and read the choice
Ask for the category
Ask for the amount inside try
If ValueError, explain and ask again
Open the file in append mode with 'with'
Write 'category,amount' and a newline
Confirm 'Saved' to the user

quiz.q: Where do you start reading a traceback?
quiz.why: Read a traceback from the bottom. The last line states the actual error and its message.

quiz.q: int('fifty') raises…
quiz.why: int('fifty') gets a string, which is the right type, but its value can't be converted to a number. That raises a ValueError.

quiz.q: Which file mode erases existing content?
quiz.why: Mode 'w' truncates (erases) the file before writing. Use 'a' to add to the end instead.

quiz.q: Why use 'with open(...) as f'?
quiz.why: The 'with' statement closes the file automatically, even if an error happens in the block.

quiz.q: Why avoid a bare 'except:'?
quiz.why: A bare 'except:' catches every error, including unexpected ones, which hides real bugs. Catch the specific errors you expect.

questions.q: print(type(3.0)) shows…
questions.why: 3.0 has a decimal point, so its type is float.

questions.q: Which symbol starts a comment?
questions.why: Python comments start with #. The other symbols are used in other languages.

questions.q: 10 / 4 in Python 3 gives…
questions.why: In Python 3, / is true division and always returns a float, so 10 / 4 is 2.5.

questions.q: Which keyword defines a function?
questions.why: def is the keyword for defining a function: def name(params):.

questions.q: x = [1, 2, 3]; x.append(4); len(x)?
questions.why: append adds one item at the end, so the list [1, 2, 3, 4] has length 4.

questions.q: for i in range(2, 10, 3): print(i) prints…
questions.why: range(2, 10, 3) starts at 2 and steps by 3, stopping before 10: 2, 5, 8.

questions.q: d = {'a': 1}; d.get('b', 0) returns…
questions.why: d.get('b', 0) returns the default 0 because the key 'b' is missing. It doesn't raise a KeyError.

questions.q: A function prints a value but has no return. Its call evaluates to…
questions.why: Printing is not returning. A function with no return statement evaluates to None.

questions.q: 'abc'[1] is…
questions.why: Strings are indexed from 0, so 'abc'[1] is the second letter, 'b'.

questions.q: What does [w.upper() for w in ['hi', 'yo'] if 'h' in w] produce?
questions.why: The loop only takes words that contain 'h'. Only 'hi' does, and it is made uppercase, giving ['HI'].

questions.q: a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a)?
questions.why: b = a doesn't copy the list. a and b are the same object, so appending to b changes a: [1, 2, 3].

questions.q: Which exception does {}['x'] raise?
questions.why: Reading a missing key from a dictionary raises a KeyError.

questions.q: def f(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else n * f(n - 1). f(5)?
questions.why: The function is the recursive factorial: f(5) = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

questions.q: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 False in Python?
options: Binary floating point cannot represent these decimals exactly
questions.why: Floats are binary approximations; compare with a tolerance (math.isclose) or use the decimal module.

questions.q: sorted({'a': 3, 'b': 1}.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]) gives…
questions.why: The lambda sorts the (key, value) pairs by value, from smallest to largest. So ('b', 1) comes before ('a', 3).

courses.title: JavaScript from zero: make web pages come alive
courses.summary: Learn the language of the web: values and variables, functions, arrays and objects, the DOM and events, and asynchronous code with fetch — using only a browser.
outcomes: Learners can declare variables with let and const and explain JavaScript's types and equality
Learners can write functions, including arrow functions, and use array methods
Learners can change a web page in response to user events
Learners can fetch JSON data asynchronously and handle errors

lessons.title: Hello, browser: values, let and const

scenes.text: Zoya, a Class 11 student in Bhopal, wanted a web page showing how many days remain until her best friend Ishita's birthday.
She learned that every browser already contains a JavaScript engine. No installation needed: press F12, open the Console, and type.
Her first line: const today = new Date(); Her second: console.log(today). The date appeared. She was programming.

steps.title: Where JavaScript runs
steps.body:
JavaScript (JS) runs in every web browser and also on servers (Node.js). To start:
- Open any browser, press F12 (or right-click → Inspect) and choose **Console**.
- Type console.log('Namaste'); and press Enter.

In a web page, put code in a file app.js and load it from HTML with a script tag: <script src='app.js' defer></script>. The defer attribute runs it after the page is built.

steps.title: let, const (and why not var)
steps.body:
const name = 'Zoya';   // cannot be reassigned
let age = 16;           // can change
age = 17;

- Prefer **const**; use **let** only when the value must change.
- **var** is the old way: it ignores block scope and causes surprises. Modern code avoids it.
- Statements usually end with ; (optional in many cases, but be consistent).

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **number** (one type for whole and decimal: 42, 3.14)
- **string** ('hi', "hi", or a template literal in backticks: `Hi ${name}`)
- **boolean** (true/false)
- **undefined** (declared but no value), **null** (intentionally empty)
- **object** (including arrays and functions)
- also bigint and symbol (advanced)
Check with typeof: typeof 42 → 'number'.

steps.title: == vs === (always use ===)
steps.body:
== converts types before comparing, which gives strange results:
'5' == 5    // true
0 == ''     // true
'5' === 5   // false

**=== checks value AND type.** Use it every time. Similarly, '5' + 1 gives '51' (string joining) while '5' - 1 gives 4. Convert explicitly: Number('5').

steps.title: Worked example: days until a birthday
Try this
steps.body: In the console: make const price = 499 and let qty = 3. Log a template string like `Total: Rs ${price * qty}`. Then test '7' + 3, '7' - 3 and '7' === 7 and explain each result to yourself.

statements.s: '5' === 5 is true.
statements.why: === also compares type; a string is not a number.

statements.s: A const variable can be reassigned later.
statements.why: const prevents reassignment (though an object's contents can still change).

statements.s: new Date(2025, 0, 1) is 1 January 2025.
statements.why: Months are 0-based, so 0 = January.

statements.s: '10' - 2 evaluates to 8.
statements.why: The minus operator converts the string to a number.

statements.s: typeof null returns 'null'.
statements.why: A long-standing quirk: typeof null is 'object'.

quiz.q: Which keyword should you use by default for a variable?
quiz.why: Use const by default and only use let when you need to reassign the variable. This avoids accidental changes.

quiz.q: '3' + 4 in JavaScript gives…
quiz.why: With a string on one side, + concatenates, so '3' + 4 is the string '34'. It doesn't add the numbers.

quiz.q: Template strings use…
quiz.why: Template strings use backticks (`), which allow ${ } to put values inside text.

quiz.q: Where can you quickly try JS without installing anything?
quiz.why: Every modern browser has a developer console (open it with F12), where you can try JavaScript without installing anything.

quiz.q: What does the defer attribute on a script tag do?
options: Runs it after the HTML is parsed
quiz.why: The defer attribute makes the browser download the script while parsing and run it after the HTML is parsed. It doesn't block the page.

lessons.title: Functions, arrays and objects

scenes.text: Kiran coaches an under-14 cricket team in Indore and keeps each player's runs in a spreadsheet.
He wanted a little web tool that showed each player's average and the top scorer.
His developer friend Laila said: 'Store each player as an object, put them in an array, and let array methods like map, filter and reduce do the work.'

steps.title: Functions three ways
Arrays
steps.body:
const runs = [45, 12, 78, 0, 33];
runs[0];          // 45
runs.length;      // 5
runs.push(50);    // add to end
runs.includes(78) // true

**Array methods take a function:**
- map → transform each item: runs.map(r => r * 2)
- filter → keep items that pass: runs.filter(r => r >= 30)
- reduce → combine into one value: runs.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r, 0)
- find, some, every, sort, forEach

steps.title: Objects and JSON
steps.body:
const player = { name: 'Aman', innings: [45, 12, 78], keeper: false };
player.name           // 'Aman'
player['keeper']      // false
player.age = 13;      // add a property
const { name, innings } = player;   // destructuring

**JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation) is the text format of objects used across the web: JSON.stringify(obj) → text, JSON.parse(text) → object. In JSON, keys must use double quotes.

steps.title: Worked example: averages and top scorer
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9] — sort compares as **text** by default. Use sort((a, b) => a - b).
- Forgetting reduce's starting value (0) on an empty array throws an error.
- An arrow function returning an object needs brackets: p => ({ ...p }).
- const arr = []; arr.push(1) is allowed — const stops reassignment, not mutation.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Using the team array: list the names of players with any century (some(r => r >= 100)), and the total runs of the whole team using map and reduce together.

activity.prompt: Match the array method to what it does.
pairs: Makes a new array by transforming every item
Keeps only items that pass a test
Combines all items into one value
True if at least one item passes
True only if all items pass

quiz.q: [1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 10) returns…
quiz.why: map applies the function to each element and returns a new array: [10, 20, 30].

quiz.q: [5, 8, 2].filter(x => x > 4) returns…
quiz.why: filter keeps elements that pass the test. Only 5 and 8 are greater than 4, so the result is [5, 8].

quiz.q: [3, 4].reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0) returns…
quiz.why: reduce starts at 0 and adds each item: 0 + 3 + 4 = 7.

quiz.q: [25, 100, 3].sort() with no comparator returns…
quiz.why: Default sort compares as text: '100' < '25' < '3'. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numeric order.

quiz.q: JSON keys must be written with…
quiz.why: JSON is stricter than JavaScript object syntax. Keys and string values must use double quotes.

lessons.title: The DOM and events: interactive pages

scenes.text: Neel, an accountant in Ahmedabad, kept forgetting to drink water at work.
He built a page with one button: each click added a glass to a counter and changed the colour as he got closer to 8 glasses.
It took 20 lines of JavaScript. 'The page listens to me,' he told his daughter. 'That's called an event listener,' she said.

steps.title: What is the DOM?
Events
Worked example: the full water tracker
Security: textContent vs innerHTML
steps.body: Never put user-typed text into **innerHTML**. If someone types an image tag with an onerror attribute containing code, innerHTML will run it — this is **cross-site scripting (XSS)**. Use textContent (treats everything as plain text) or build elements with document.createElement.

steps.title: Forms without page reloads
Try this
steps.body: Build a to-do list: an input, an Add button and a list. On submit, create a list item with createElement, set its textContent, and append it. Bonus: clicking an item toggles a 'done' class; save the list to localStorage as JSON.

activity.prompt: Order what happens when Neel clicks the button.
items: The browser detects a click on the button
It calls the registered callback function
glasses increases by 1
The new value is saved to localStorage
render() updates the paragraph's textContent
The browser repaints the page

quiz.q: The DOM is…
options: A tree of objects representing the page
quiz.why: The DOM (Document Object Model) is a tree of objects that represents the page. The browser builds it from the HTML.

quiz.q: document.querySelector('.count') selects…
options: The first element with class count
quiz.why: querySelector('.count') finds the first element with class 'count'. A dot means class, while # means id.

quiz.q: Safest way to show user input on a page?
quiz.why: textContent treats the text as plain text and never runs HTML or scripts. innerHTML can run malicious code, so it is unsafe for user input.

quiz.q: Why call e.preventDefault() in a submit handler?
options: To stop the default page reload
quiz.why: A form submit reloads the page by default. e.preventDefault() stops that, so your JavaScript can handle the data.

quiz.q: localStorage stores values as…
quiz.why: localStorage stores everything as strings. To store objects, convert them with JSON.stringify and read them back with JSON.parse.

lessons.title: Asynchronous JavaScript: fetch, promises, async/await

scenes.text: Sana, an MCA student in Srinagar, wanted her portfolio page to show live weather from a free public API.
Her first attempt printed 'undefined': the data had not arrived when her code tried to use it.

She learned that network calls are asynchronous: JavaScript keeps going and comes back when the answer arrives. With async/await her widget worked — and showed a friendly message when the network failed.

steps.title: Why asynchronous?
steps.body: A network request may take 50 ms or 5 seconds. JavaScript in the browser runs your code on a single main thread; if it waited, the page would freeze. Instead, slow operations return a **Promise** — an object that will later be *fulfilled* with a value or *rejected* with an error. The **event loop** runs your callback when the result is ready.

steps.title: Worked example: fetch with async/await
Order of execution puzzle
Running requests in parallel
steps.body:
const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetch(url1), fetch(url2)]);
Promise.all waits for all and fails fast if any fails. Promise.allSettled gives every result, success or failure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting await → you log a Promise object instead of data.
- Using await outside an async function (allowed only at the top level of ES modules).
- Not handling errors → a silent failure for the user. Always show a helpful message.
- **CORS errors:** the browser blocks reading responses from servers that do not allow your site's origin. That is a server setting, not a bug in your fetch code.
- Never put secret API keys in browser JavaScript — anyone can read them.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write wait(ms) that returns new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)). Then write an async function that logs 3, 2, 1, 'Go!' one second apart using await wait(1000).

a.text: Sana's widget shows 'undefined' instead of the temperature. Her code: const data = fetch(url).json(); What is wrong?

choices.label: fetch returns a Promise; she must await it
choices.feedback: Correct — the response is not there yet.

choices.label: The API is broken
choices.feedback: Possible, but check your own code first — the symptom points to a missing await.

b.text: She writes const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json(); Now, during testing, the API returns 404. What happens?

choices.label: fetch rejects and catch runs
choices.feedback: Not quite — fetch resolves on 404. Only network errors reject.

choices.label: fetch resolves; she must check res.ok
choices.feedback: Yes! Check res.ok and throw a meaningful error.

c.text: She opens DevTools → Network and sees a successful 200 response. So the API is fine and the bug is in her code.

choices.label: Look again at how the promise is used
choices.feedback: Good debugging: evidence before blame.

c2.text: Her catch block never runs, and the page shows broken data. She rereads the fetch documentation.

choices.label: Add if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...)
choices.feedback: Now HTTP errors reach the catch block.

d.text: The widget shows the temperature, or 'Weather unavailable, try later' if anything fails. Robust async code: await every promise, check res.ok, catch errors, tell the user.

quiz.q: What does fetch() return immediately?
quiz.why: fetch() immediately returns a Promise that will later give a Response. It doesn't return the data directly.

quiz.q: Does fetch reject on HTTP 404?
quiz.why: fetch only rejects on network failure. An HTTP 404 still resolves, so you must check res.ok.

quiz.q: Output order: log A; setTimeout B 0; Promise.then C; log D
quiz.why: Synchronous code runs first (A, then D). Then microtasks like Promise.then (C), and finally timers (B). So the order is A D C B.

quiz.q: Promise.all fails when…
quiz.why: Promise.all rejects as soon as any one of the promises rejects. It fails fast on the first rejection.

quiz.q: Why not put secret API keys in browser JS?
options: Anyone can view the source and steal them
quiz.why: Browser JavaScript can be read by anyone through the page source, so secret API keys would be stolen. Keep secrets on a server.

questions.q: Which keyword declares a variable that cannot be reassigned?
questions.why: const declares a variable that cannot be reassigned. let allows reassignment.

questions.q: Which method prints to the browser console?
questions.why: console.log() prints to the browser console. print() is for Python and System.out is for Java.

questions.q: Which equality operator should you normally use?
questions.why: === compares value and type without type coercion, so it is the normal choice. == can give surprising results.

questions.q: [1, 2, 3].length is…
questions.why: The array [1, 2, 3] has three items, so its length is 3.

questions.q: Which event fires when a button is pressed?
questions.why: The click event fires when a button is pressed (clicked).

questions.q: const f = x => x + 1; f(4)?
questions.why: The arrow function returns x + 1, so f(4) is 5.

questions.q: JSON.parse('{"a":1}').a is…
questions.why: JSON.parse turns JSON text into an object, so .a is the number 1.

questions.q: Which is safer for inserting user text into the page?
questions.why: textContent is safer, because it inserts plain text and never runs HTML or scripts. innerHTML can allow cross-site scripting (XSS).

questions.q: new Date(2024, 11, 25) is…
questions.why: In JavaScript Date, months count from 0, so month 11 is December. new Date(2024, 11, 25) is 25 December 2024.

questions.q: [10, 1, 5].sort((a, b) => a - b) gives…
questions.why: The comparator (a, b) => a − b sorts numbers in ascending order: [1, 5, 10]. The default sort compares text.

questions.q: What does await do?
options: Pauses the async function until the promise settles
questions.why: await pauses the async function until the promise settles. Other code and the UI keep running, so it doesn't block the browser.

questions.q: Which runs first: a resolved Promise's .then callback or a setTimeout(…, 0) callback?
questions.why: A resolved Promise's .then callback is a microtask, and microtasks run before the next task, such as setTimeout, even with 0 delay.

questions.q: Result of [1, 2, 3].reduce((a, x) => a + x)?
questions.why: With no initial value, the first element is the start: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 (it errors only on an empty array).

questions.q: A fetch to another domain fails with a CORS error. Most accurate explanation?
options: The server did not allow your origin, so the browser blocked the response
questions.why: CORS is enforced by the browser. If the server's headers don't allow your origin, the browser blocks your code from reading the response.

courses.title: Object-oriented design, testing, debugging and Git
courses.summary: Move from scripts to software: classes and objects, inheritance versus composition, automated tests, systematic debugging, and working with Git and pull requests like a professional team.
outcomes: Learners can model real things as classes with attributes and methods
Learners can choose between inheritance and composition and explain encapsulation and polymorphism
Learners can write unit tests and debug with breakpoints and logs
Learners can use Git branches, commits, merges and pull requests safely

lessons.title: Classes and objects

story.title: The bank-account bug at Rupa's startup

scenes.text: Rupa built a savings app for self-help groups in Odisha. Balances were stored in loose variables and dictionaries all over the code.
One day a function subtracted a withdrawal without checking the balance. A member's balance went to minus Rs 3,000.
Her mentor Thomas suggested an Account class: balance can only change through deposit() and withdraw(), and withdraw() refuses to overdraw.
The rule now lived in one place. The bug could never come back.

steps.title: Class = blueprint, object = thing
What is self?
steps.body: **self** is the particular object a method is working on. meena.deposit(200) is really Account.deposit(meena, 200). __init__ is the **constructor**: it runs automatically when you create an object and sets its starting attributes.

steps.title: Encapsulation
steps.body: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data and the rules that protect it together, and exposing a small, safe interface. The leading underscore in _balance is a Python *convention* meaning 'internal — do not touch from outside'. Python does not strictly enforce privacy; Java and C# use private/public keywords. The @property lets people *read* balance without being able to set it directly.

steps.title: Worked example: the same idea in JavaScript
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting self as the first parameter of a method → TypeError about arguments.
- Writing balance = 0 instead of self.balance = 0 inside __init__ (creates a local variable that disappears).
- Using a mutable default: def __init__(self, items=[]) shares ONE list among all objects. Use items=None and create a new list inside.
- Making classes for everything. A simple function is often better.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a class LibraryBook with title, is_borrowed and methods borrow() and give_back(). borrow() should raise an error if already borrowed. Create two books and test both paths.

activity.prompt: Complete the constructor.

quiz.q: A class is to an object as…
options: A recipe is to a dish
A dish is to a recipe
quiz.why: A class is a blueprint, like a recipe, and objects are made from it, like dishes. So class is to object as recipe is to dish.

quiz.q: What does self refer to?
quiz.why: self refers to the current object, the instance on which the method was called.

quiz.q: Why route all balance changes through methods?
options: To enforce rules like 'no overdraft' in one place
quiz.why: Routing balance changes through methods lets you enforce rules like 'no overdraft' in one place. This is encapsulation.

quiz.q: def __init__(self, items=[]) is risky because…
options: All objects share the same default list
quiz.why: A default value like items=[] is created once, when the function is defined. So all objects share the same list, which can cause surprising bugs.

quiz.q: In JavaScript, a class field starting with # is…
quiz.why: In JavaScript, a field starting with # is truly private. It cannot be accessed from outside the class.

lessons.title: Inheritance, composition and polymorphism

story.title: Delivery vehicles at Joseph's logistics firm

scenes.text: Joseph's logistics company in Kochi uses bikes, vans and trucks. Each has a different cost per km and load limit.
His developer Aisha first made Bike, Van and Truck all inherit from Vehicle. That worked — until electric vans needed a battery and diesel trucks needed fuel, and the class tree became a tangle.
She refactored: each vehicle has an engine object (Electric or Diesel). 'Favour composition over inheritance,' she told the team.

steps.title: Inheritance: is-a
Polymorphism
steps.body:
fleet = [Bike('KL-07-1', 20), Truck('KL-07-9', 9000)]
for v in fleet:
    print(v.reg, v.cost(10))

The same call v.cost(10) does the right thing for each type. Code that uses vehicles does not need if type == 'bike' checks. This is **polymorphism**: one interface, many forms. In Python it also works through **duck typing** — any object with a cost() method fits, even without a common parent.

steps.title: Composition: has-a
SOLID in one line each
steps.body:
- **S**ingle responsibility: one reason to change per class.
- **O**pen/closed: extend behaviour without editing tested code.
- **L**iskov substitution: a subclass must work anywhere its parent is expected.
- **I**nterface segregation: many small interfaces beat one giant one.
- **D**ependency inversion: depend on abstractions (an 'engine' with cost_per_km), not concrete classes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inheriting just to reuse a helper method (use a function or composition).
- Deep chains (A → B → C → D) — a change at the top breaks everything below.
- A subclass that breaks promises the parent makes (violates Liskov). Classic example: a Square inheriting from a mutable Rectangle, where code that sets width and height independently gets surprising results.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Add a Drone class with a battery and a max range of 15 km. Make cost() raise an error if km is beyond range. Does Drone inherit from Vehicle, or compose a Battery, or both? Write down your reason.

activity.prompt: Is-a (inheritance) or has-a (composition)?

items.text: A Manager and an Employee (same HR record type)

quiz.q: Polymorphism means…
options: One interface, different behaviour per type
quiz.why: Polymorphism means one interface with different behaviour for each type. The same method call works differently depending on the object.

quiz.q: 'Favour composition over inheritance' mainly helps to…
quiz.why: Composition builds objects from parts, which avoids rigid, deep inheritance hierarchies. Parts can be swapped independently.

quiz.q: Overriding means…
options: Redefining a parent's method in the subclass
quiz.why: Overriding means a subclass redefines a method of its parent, supplying its own version.

quiz.q: Which SOLID principle says a subclass must work wherever its parent does?
quiz.why: The Liskov substitution principle says that a subclass must work wherever its parent class is expected.

quiz.q: super().__init__(reg, max_kg) does what?
options: Runs the parent class's constructor for this object
quiz.why: super().__init__(...) runs the parent class's constructor for this same object, so the parent's setup is reused. It doesn't create a new parent object.

lessons.title: Testing and systematic debugging

scenes.text: At an e-commerce company in Gurugram, a discount function crashed on the first morning of a Diwali sale: 100% discount items caused a divide-by-zero in the 'savings ratio'.
Engineer Mohit reproduced it in a few minutes with a unit test and fixed it in one line.
The test stayed in the codebase forever. 'A bug fixed without a test is a bug that will return,' his lead Shalini said.

steps.title: Unit tests
What to test
steps.body:
- **Happy path:** typical inputs.
- **Edge cases:** 0, empty list, 100%, the largest value, negative numbers, very long strings.
- **Error cases:** invalid input raises the right error.
- **Regression tests:** every bug you fix gets a test that would have caught it.

The **test pyramid**: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests (several parts together), very few slow end-to-end UI tests.

steps.title: Debugging like a scientist
steps.body:
- **Reproduce** reliably, ideally as a failing test.
- **Read the error and stack trace** fully.
- **Form a hypothesis** ('pct = 100 makes the denominator zero').
- **Inspect:** use a debugger (breakpoint() in Python, the Sources panel in browser DevTools, editor breakpoints) to pause and examine variables; or add temporary logs.
- **Narrow down:** binary search — disable half, or use git bisect to find the commit that introduced the bug.
- **Fix, then run all tests.**

steps.title: Logging, not print, in real systems
steps.body:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info('Applying discount %s to %s', pct, sku)

Logs have levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR), timestamps, and can be searched later in production. Never log passwords, OTPs, card numbers or personal data.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tests that depend on each other or on the current time/network → flaky. Make tests independent and deterministic.
- Testing implementation details instead of behaviour; refactors then break tests needlessly.
- Comparing floats with == in tests; use pytest.approx.
- 'Works on my machine' — reproduce in a clean environment (same versions, same data).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write three tests for an is_valid_pincode(s) function (Indian PIN codes are 6 digits and do not start with 0). Test '560001' (valid), '056001' (invalid), '56000' (too short), and 'ABCDEF'. Then write the function until all pass — this order is called **test-driven development (TDD)**.

activity.prompt: Order a disciplined bug fix.
items: Reproduce the bug reliably
Write a failing test that shows it
Read the stack trace and form a hypothesis
Inspect with a debugger or logs to confirm
Make the smallest fix
Run the whole test suite
Commit the fix with the test and a clear message

quiz.q: A regression test is…
options: A test that guards against a fixed bug returning
quiz.why: A regression test guards against a bug that was fixed from coming back. It keeps old bugs fixed.

quiz.q: Which belongs at the wide base of the test pyramid?
quiz.why: Unit tests form the wide base of the test pyramid because they are fast, cheap and numerous. End-to-end tests sit near the top.

quiz.q: git bisect helps you…
options: Find which commit introduced a bug
quiz.why: git bisect does a binary search through your commits to find which one introduced a bug.

quiz.q: Why are unit tests that call a real external API often flaky?
options: Network and data can change, making results unpredictable
quiz.why: A real external API depends on the network and on data that can change, so results are unpredictable and tests can be flaky. Use mocks or fakes for unit tests.

quiz.q: Which should NEVER be written to logs?
quiz.why: Passwords and OTPs must never be logged, because logs are widely accessible. Secrets and personal data should stay out of them.

lessons.title: Git and GitHub: teamwork without chaos

scenes.text: Four engineering students in Nagpur — Tanvi, Imran, Chris and Pallavi — were building their final-year project by emailing zip files named final_v7_REAL.zip.
Two days before the demo, Imran's zip overwrote Tanvi's login feature. Nobody knew which version was correct.
A senior showed them Git: every change is a commit with a message; each person works on a branch; changes come together through reviewed pull requests.
Once they were using Git, nobody's work was overwritten again, and they finished calmly.

steps.title: What Git does
steps.body:
**Git** is a distributed version control system. It records snapshots (**commits**) of your project, so you can see who changed what and why, go back in time, and work in parallel safely. **GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure Repos** are hosting services that add pull requests, reviews and CI on top of Git.

Three areas: **working directory** (your files) → **staging area** (what will go into the next commit) → **repository** (committed history).

steps.title: Worked example: the everyday loop
steps.body:
git init                      # or: git clone <url>
git status                    # what changed?
git add app.py                # stage a file
git commit -m 'Add login form validation'
git log --oneline             # see history

git switch -c feature/login   # new branch (older: git checkout -b)
# …edit, add, commit…
git push -u origin feature/login
# open a Pull Request on GitHub → review → merge
git switch main
git pull                      # get the merged result

steps.title: Merging and conflicts
steps.body:
When two branches change the **same lines**, Git cannot decide and marks a **conflict** in the file between <<<<<<< HEAD, ======= and >>>>>>> branch-name markers — your version above, theirs below.

You edit the file to the correct final version, delete the markers, then git add and git commit. Talk to your teammate when unsure — conflicts are a communication signal, not a disaster.

steps.title: Professional habits
steps.body:
- Small commits with messages that say *why*: 'Fix crash when discount is 100%'.
- Pull often to reduce conflicts.
- Never commit secrets (.env files, keys). Add them to **.gitignore**. If a secret is pushed, treat it as leaked: **revoke/rotate it** — deleting the file later does not remove it from history.
- Protect main: require pull-request reviews and passing tests before merging.

steps.title: Undo safely
steps.body:
- git restore file.py → discard uncommitted changes in a file.
- git revert <commit> → make a new commit that undoes an old one (safe on shared branches).
- git reset --hard → throws away work; never use it on commits others have pulled.
- git push --force on a shared branch can erase teammates' work. If you must, prefer --force-with-lease, and only on your own branch.
- git reflog lists recent positions of HEAD — the safety net to recover 'lost' commits.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a repo, commit a README, make a branch, change the same line on both branches, merge, and resolve the conflict yourself. Doing it once on purpose removes the fear forever.

a.text: You accidentally committed config.env containing a database password and pushed it to a public GitHub repo. What first?

choices.label: Delete the file in a new commit and move on
choices.feedback: Not enough — the password is still in history and may already be copied by bots that scan public repos.

choices.label: Rotate (change) the password immediately, then clean up
choices.feedback: Correct: assume the secret is compromised. Rotation is the real fix.

b.text: A week later the database shows logins from an unknown IP. The old password was scraped from history.

choices.label: Rotate the password now and review access logs
choices.feedback: Better late than never — and report it to your security team.

c.text: Password rotated. Now how do you stop this happening again?

choices.label: Add *.env to .gitignore and use a secret manager or CI secrets
choices.feedback: Yes — plus enable secret scanning / push protection if your platform offers it.

choices.label: Make the repo private and keep secrets in it
choices.feedback: Private repos still leak (forks, laptops, ex-members). Secrets belong in a secret store.

e.text: A teammate's laptop with a clone is stolen. Every secret in the repo is exposed again.

choices.label: Move secrets to a proper secret store
choices.feedback: Lesson learned.

d.text: Secrets now live in environment variables / a vault, .gitignore blocks .env files, and pushes are scanned. You handled a real incident the professional way.

quiz.q: The staging area holds…
options: Changes chosen for the next commit
quiz.why: The staging area holds the changes you chose for the next commit. git add puts changes there.

quiz.q: Safest way to undo a commit already pushed to a shared branch?
quiz.why: git revert adds a new commit that undoes the old one and keeps the history intact. That is safe for shared branches, unlike a reset or force push.

quiz.q: A merge conflict happens when…
options: Two branches change the same lines differently
quiz.why: A merge conflict happens when two branches change the same lines in different ways. Git can't choose, so a human must resolve it.

quiz.q: Which file tells Git which files to ignore?
quiz.why: .gitignore lists the files and patterns Git should ignore, such as secrets or build files.

quiz.q: You pushed an API key. Deleting it in the next commit is enough. True?
quiz.why: This is false. The key stays in the Git history, where anyone can find it. You must rotate (replace) the key.

questions.q: An object is…
questions.why: An object is an instance of a class: a specific thing made from the blueprint.

questions.q: Which command records staged changes in Git?
questions.why: git commit records the staged changes as a snapshot. git add only stages them.

questions.q: Inheritance models which relationship?
questions.why: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship: a Truck is a Vehicle. 'Has-a' is composition.

questions.q: What does a unit test check?
options: The whole system end to end
A small piece of code in isolation
questions.why: A unit test checks a small piece of code, such as a function, in isolation.

questions.q: git switch -c fix/login does what?
options: Creates and switches to a new branch
questions.why: git switch -c fix/login creates a new branch called fix/login and switches to it. The -c means create.

questions.q: Encapsulation is…
options: Bundling data with the methods that protect it behind a small interface
questions.why: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that protect it, and exposes only a small interface. The rules are then enforced in one place.

questions.q: Why might 'git push --force' be dangerous?
options: It can overwrite commits others already pushed
questions.why: git push --force can overwrite commits that others already pushed, because it replaces the remote history.

questions.q: TDD order is…
options: Write a failing test, make it pass, refactor
questions.why: Test-driven development goes red, green, refactor: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code.

questions.q: Which is composition?
questions.why: Composition means one object has another as a part. self.engine = Engine() inside Car means a car has an engine.

questions.q: Python: class A: x = []. a1, a2 = A(), A(); a1.x.append(1). a2.x is…
questions.why: x = [] is a class attribute, shared by all instances. a1.x.append(1) changes the same list, so a2.x is [1].

questions.q: Which command helps recover a commit you 'lost' after a bad reset?
questions.why: git reflog records where HEAD has been, so you can find a commit 'lost' after a reset and recover it.

questions.q: A Square subclass of a mutable Rectangle breaks callers that set width and height independently. This violates…
questions.why: A Square cannot replace a mutable Rectangle when callers set width and height independently. It can't stand in for its parent, which violates the Liskov substitution principle.

questions.q: A test passes locally but fails randomly in CI. Most likely cause?
options: Tests should not run in CI
The test depends on time, order or network — it is non-deterministic
questions.why: A test that passes locally but fails randomly in CI is flaky. It usually has a hidden dependency on time, order or network, so it is non-deterministic.

questions.q: In dependency inversion, a Van should depend on…
options: An abstraction such as 'something with cost_per_km()'
questions.why: Dependency inversion says to depend on abstractions, such as 'something with cost_per_km()', not on a concrete DieselEngine. Then the engine can change without changing the Van.

tech-security-devops.title: Cybersecurity and DevOps
tech-security-devops.description: Protect people and systems — the CIA triad, threats, phishing, cryptography, OWASP Top 10 and Security+-style operations — and ship software safely with CI/CD, containers, Kubernetes and infrastructure as code.

courses.title: Cybersecurity foundations for everyone
courses.summary: The core ideas of security in plain language: the CIA triad, common threats and malware, phishing and scams (with India's reporting options), passwords and multi-factor authentication, and the cryptography that protects everyday life. Topic tags show which syllabus this can support. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can explain confidentiality, integrity, availability and AAA with examples
Learners can recognise common malware and social-engineering attacks
Learners can spot phishing and UPI/OTP scams and know how to report cybercrime in India
Learners can explain hashing, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures and TLS

lessons.title: The CIA triad: what security protects

scenes.text: At a school in Ranchi, a spreadsheet of Class 10 pre-board marks was accidentally shared to a public link. Parents saw other children's marks.
Days later, someone with the link quietly changed a few marks. Then the school's website went down on results day under heavy traffic.
The computer teacher, Mr. Minz, used it to teach his class: 'Three different failures. Confidentiality broken by the leak, integrity broken by the edits, availability broken by the outage.'

steps.title: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
steps.body:
- **Confidentiality:** only the right people can see information. Tools: access control, encryption, classification ('internal', 'confidential').
- **Integrity:** information is accurate and not changed without authorisation. Tools: permissions, hashing, digital signatures, version history, audit logs.
- **Availability:** systems and data are there when needed. Tools: backups, redundancy, capacity planning, DDoS protection, patching.
Most security decisions balance these three. Locking a file so tightly that doctors cannot open it in an emergency protects confidentiality but harms availability.

steps.title: AAA and non-repudiation
steps.body:
- **Authentication:** proving who you are (password, OTP, fingerprint).
- **Authorisation:** what you are allowed to do once identified (read marks vs edit marks).
- **Accounting (auditing):** recording who did what and when (logs).
- **Non-repudiation:** someone cannot credibly deny an action they took — e.g. a digitally signed document.

steps.title: Risk in one line
steps.body:
**Risk ≈ likelihood × impact.** A threat (someone or something that could cause harm) exploits a vulnerability (a weakness) to damage an asset (something of value).
Responses to a risk: **mitigate** (add controls), **transfer** (insurance, outsourcing), **avoid** (stop the risky activity), **accept** (consciously live with it).

steps.title: Worked example: fixing the school's problems
steps.body:
- Confidentiality: share marks only with named staff accounts, never 'anyone with the link'; parents see only their own child's marks through a login.
- Integrity: only the exam cell can edit; keep version history; log every change.
- Availability: host results on a service that can scale; publish a backup PDF link; test with expected traffic beforehand.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of your phone. Write one threat to each of its confidentiality, integrity and availability, and one control you already use (or should) for each.

activity.prompt: Which part of the CIA triad was mainly harmed?

items.text: A hacker reads customers' Aadhaar-linked records
Someone edits bank account numbers in invoices
An email with salary data goes to the wrong person
A website crashes during a flash sale
Exam marks are changed without permission

quiz.q: Encryption mainly protects…
quiz.why: Encryption protects confidentiality: only someone with the key can read the data.

quiz.q: Backups mainly protect…
quiz.why: Backups mainly protect availability, because you can restore data after loss. They also help recover integrity after damage.

quiz.q: Checking what a logged-in user may do is…
quiz.why: Checking what a logged-in user is allowed to do is authorisation. Authentication is proving who they are.

quiz.q: Buying cyber insurance is an example of risk…
quiz.why: Buying cyber insurance shifts the financial impact to the insurer, which is risk transfer.

quiz.q: Logs that record who changed a mark support…
quiz.why: Logs that record who changed a mark support accounting (auditing), because actions can be traced to a person.

lessons.title: Threats: malware and social engineering

scenes.text: Accountant Manoj in a Kanpur textile firm received a WhatsApp message: 'Your courier is on hold. Download the delivery form.' The file was named Delivery_Form.apk.
He installed it. The app asked for SMS permission. Within hours, OTPs were being read and small amounts drained from linked wallets.
The firm's IT person, Fatima, wiped the phone, reset passwords and helped him report it. Then she trained the whole office: unexpected files, urgency and requests for permissions are red flags.

steps.title: Malware types
steps.body:
- **Virus:** attaches to files/programs and spreads when they run.
- **Worm:** spreads by itself across networks, without user action.
- **Trojan:** looks legitimate (a 'delivery form' app) but hides malicious functions.
- **Ransomware:** encrypts or steals data and demands payment.
- **Spyware / keylogger:** secretly collects information or keystrokes.
- **Rootkit:** hides deep in the system to keep privileged access.
- **Botnet:** many infected devices controlled remotely, e.g. for DDoS attacks or spam.
- **Fileless malware:** runs in memory or abuses legitimate tools, leaving fewer traces.

steps.title: Social engineering
steps.body:
Attackers manipulate people rather than machines, using **urgency, fear, authority, curiosity or greed**.
- **Phishing** (email), **smishing** (SMS), **vishing** (voice calls), plus messaging apps.
- **Spear phishing:** targeted at a specific person using personal details; **whaling:** targets senior executives.
- **Pretexting:** an invented story ('I'm from your bank's KYC team').
- **Baiting:** a free USB drive or a 'free movie' download.
- **Tailgating/piggybacking:** following someone through a secure door.
- **Business email compromise:** fake or hijacked email from a 'vendor' changing bank details.

steps.title: Other common attacks
steps.body:
- **Denial of service (DoS/DDoS):** overwhelm a service so real users can't reach it.
- **Man-in-the-middle / on-path:** intercepting traffic, e.g. on fake Wi-Fi.
- **Credential stuffing:** using leaked passwords from one site on others.
- **Brute force / password spraying:** guessing many passwords, or one common password across many accounts.
- **Supply-chain attacks:** compromising software or vendors that many organisations trust.
- **Zero-day:** exploiting a vulnerability before a fix exists.

steps.title: Everyday defences
steps.body:
- Install apps only from official stores; be wary of APK files sent in chats.
- Keep OS and apps updated; enable automatic updates.
- Use a password manager and **unique** passwords; turn on MFA.
- Back up important data (with one copy offline) — the best answer to ransomware.
- Pause before acting on urgent messages; verify through an official number or app.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check which apps on your phone have SMS, accessibility or 'display over other apps' permissions. Remove any you don't trust — these permissions are commonly abused by banking trojans.

activity.prompt: Match each attack to its description.
pairs: Following someone through a secure door
Reusing leaked passwords on other sites

quiz.q: Malware that spreads without any user action is a…
quiz.why: A worm spreads on its own across networks, without needing any user action. A virus usually needs a user to run something.
